The video hit a nerve: insane enough at the first sight, yet kind of rational if you know what we know now. Namespace @ namespacelabs Unboxing Macs at scale for our new server racks. 4:27 PM · Aug 24, 2026 · 25M Views 1K 964 5K 1.8K So today I want to give some background into what it takes to build custom Mac racks, how we can start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and deliver new Xcode versions mere hours after Apple releases them . So why MacBooks? Because our customers need Macs. And because Apple didn’t give us another option. Many of our customers build and test iOS apps. You can't build iOS apps without a Mac. The iOS Simulator only runs on a Mac. Moreover, in order to release an app to the App Store, Apple requires using a recent Xcode version. xtool xtool is cool, but it is not (yet) a serious replacement. So your coding agent needs a Mac. But still, why laptops? Isn’t it a major waste of screen pixels and keyboard buttons and battery ions? Well yes, Mac Mini would be a better choice for a datacenter. Sure, it has very rudimentary remote management, no redundant power, and a beautiful case that ensures that cooling will be difficult regardless of which side you lay it on. But these are all known challenges that we have learned to manage. But have you actually tried to order a couple hundred Minis? We have. Ordered in January, delivered in July. Welcome to the world of 2026 when the supply chains are in disarray. Never mind that Apple doesn’t release updated CPU models to all devices at once. So Mac Mini didn’t get M5 cores for 10 months (and then suddenly got M6 before any other device model!). We promise the best and the newest to our customers so we had to be inventive. That’s how the MacBook-in-Datacenter project was born. Our beautiful Mac racks Good design takes iterations; and we surely didn’t get everything right from the first try. But I think we have the system nailed down. Every MacBook is connected to an IP KVM for remote management. Indispensable when dealing with laptops. Unlike Mac Mini, laptop firmware is designed with the screen in mind: some maintenance actions can only be done by clicking buttons in the beautiful GUI. Of course, every MacBook gets an external 10G Ethernet NIC. Many folks at Namespace are networking geeks and we are proud of the connection speed and reliability that we provide to customers. And then there is power. So in total, four cables per laptop, forty-eight per shelf, plus twelve for Ethernet, plus KVM wiring. Let’s just say that careful cable management is essential. Heat management too. Currently we are deploying custom-made holders, designed to wick the heat from the hotspots and guide hot air away instead of blowing it at the nearby machines. Not the problems we expected: HDMI, FileVault, and USB NICs Naturally, we expected problems and challenges. Just not where they appeared. I bet some of you looked at the pic above, saw MagSafe cables plugged in and already started writing a snarky tweet that MagSafe is not safe and may get accidentally disconnected. And yes, I was worried about that too. But the reality is that we have seen very few cases of MagSafe disconnections. The most unreliable cable? HDMI! Often thick and inflexible. Tends to fall out every time you touch the shelf. Luckily by now we found almost perfect cables that bend exactly as we want them to bend. And we bought the entire supply of them. There are zero more of them available to order on Amazon. Another source of pain: FileVault disk encryption. Or rather decryption. When a MacBook reboots (in an unplanned fashion) it prompts for a password to unlock the local disk. The prompt is shown on the screen (of a closed laptop somewhere in the rack, doh). No problem, we thought: we have the KVM connected just for this case! Nope, not so easy. The password prompt disappears from the external screen after 5 minutes of inactivity. Then we remembered that macOS Tahoe introduced a useful feature: we could unlock FileVault remotely using SSH protocol. Still no luck. On laptops it expires after 5 minutes too. Looks like the only way out of this state is to reboot by physically pressing the button and racing to unlock in time. Mac reboot While on this topic, a small tip: you can reboot a Mac in a way that will keep the disk unlocked when you need it: fdesetup authrestart . And then there are simply bugs. Under certain conditions, an external USB NIC stops working and acts as if it is not powered and shows no link. Trying another cable, another NIC, another switch port, no luck. But a quick visit to Network Preferences, deleting and recreating the “network service” in MacOS Settings brings it back to life. What about Mac Minis and Studios? At the moment we actually have it easy: M5 and M6 Mac Minis and Studios are coming into our fleet soon. They are way simpler to manage in the DC: they have a built-in 10 Gb network card, they boot up automatically after a power cycle and the OS can be configured entirely automatically via MDM. But Namespace has some special sauce for the Minis too. We design custom-made shelves that hold the machines with focus on efficient cooling. We have tested a few designs using airflow simulation to arrive at what we are deploying now. In the end installing Mac Minis is a breeze: unpack them, throw 10 pieces into the holder, connect power and network and press the power button once (famously inconveniently located). From there on automation takes care of them. Virtualizing Macs Under the hood a Namespace instance is backed by a virtual machine. We have multiple virtual machine engines integrated into a unified platform to run Linux, Windows, and Mac instances in the most efficient way. This way we can provide the same features that make Namespace special, like cache volumes , telemetry, or VPC connections. Unsurprisingly, our Mac solution is based on Apple’s excellent Virtualization framework . It is an embeddable and flexible virtual machine engine. It’s easiest to compare it to Firecracker in how it fits the system architecture: it implements generic VM operations end-to-end as well as typical peripherals. macOS on Apple Virtualization Namespace VM host process Virtualization framework · like Firecracker QEMU VMM Hypervisor framework Apple · like KVM The Namespace VM host starts macOS guests through the Virtualization framework, which fits the system the way Firecracker does. Underneath is the Hypervisor framework, comparable to KVM. QEMU uses the Hypervisor framework too, but it can't run macOS. For completeness, Apple also provides a lower-level Hypervisor framework , which is comparable to the KVM API of Linux. For instance QEMU uses it on macOS under the hood. Hypervisor provides a way to execute machine code in isolation, but requires the application developer to implement the bulk of machine architecture and peripherals. It could give us a lot of control, but unfortunately it cannot run macOS (it requires an Apple proprietary environment that third parties cannot, or shouldn’t, try to recreate). In fact, most competing platforms are built on the same foundation. But the details matter: Apple gives us a few primitives that need to be arranged in just the right way to work fast and be secure. The more interesting thing is to watch how different people solve similar problems with different constraints. Limitations of Apple Virtualization A well-known limitation is that Apple only allows two macOS VMs per physical Mac. It can be a Mac Pro with 24 cores and 192 GB memory, yet it is limited to running only two guest VMs. This limitation leaks into our product offering: we can only slice Mac resources in two halves. So we run instances with 6 or 12 cores on 14-core Mac Minis and 8/16-core instances on 18-core MacBooks (we reserve a couple cores for management overhead). MacBook · 18 cores IPC roundtrips 0 2 host · 8 + 8 VMs process boundary Namespace VM host process · 2 cores Virtualization framework VM 1 · VMM process not started VM 2 · VMM process not started VM 3 Hypervisor framework Two cores stay with the Namespace VM host, and the rest split in half between the only two macOS VMs Apple allows per Mac. Each VM runs in its own VMM process, so hooking VM behavior or a custom virtual device costs an IPC roundtrip across the process boundary. On a 14-core Mac mini, the split is 2, 6 and 6. An important consideration of Virtualization VMs is that the virtual CPU is executed by a separate OS process (VMM process in the diagram) from the software integrating Virtualization (here Namespace VM host). If we want to hook some VM behavior or implement custom virtual devices, every interaction with them requires an IPC roundtrip between the VM process and the “host” process. Such context switches are unavoidable and need to be taken into account when designing the system. Virtual networking Virtualization framework offers a few ways to connect a virtual machine to the network. For instance, bridged and NAT networking modes route traffic directly from the VMM process to the host network interfaces. These are suitable for VMs running on a local computer where the workload is trusted. Namespace instances run untrusted code and we need to enforce policies on what a VM can or cannot access (these policies can also be customer-defined! ). Also we provide a few additional services to the instances that should appear “as if” they were on the local network for the guest system. This requires us to take full control of guest networking in the mode where we process every packet that comes out and into the VM in software. We based our guest networking on a userspace TCP/IP stack from Google gVisor project and use it to implement an IP gateway/firewall for the instances. This way we minimize exposure of the host OS to unprocessed packets controlled by the guest. Network packet handling needs to be very efficient, but as outlined above the path involves IPC. The VMM process needs first to pass the packets to the “VM host” process, which then processes and passes them to the network interface. It takes careful implementation and batch processing wherever possible to minimize the number of IPC roundtrips. The above approach allows Namespace MacOS instances to reach 4 Gbps upstream bandwidth (per Fast.com ). This is unfortunately still lower than the line rate. We have been exploring alternative approaches, including ideas on how to avoid IPC for network processing entirely. But productionizing the new setup is still left for the future. After all, 4 Gbps is still quite respectable. VM images Creating your first VM using Apple Virtualization is very easy: download a macOS installer XIP, use UTM/Tart/any of the dozens of open-source Virtualization wrappers to start a machine, click through Setup Assistant, install Xcode and you are good to go. Now you have a VM image that you can fork and run any workload locally. But you need to test on multiple versions of iOS, so you install a few iOS runtimes. And then you install the upcoming Xcode beta version (and new runtimes too). And before you know it your VM image has grown to 500 GB (iOS runtime packages are huge). You also want to have the previous version of macOS for testing that one little thing. Another 500 GB right here. Apple releases the new macOS developer preview, one more image. And then you realize that the Xcode beta version subtly breaks the non-beta Xcodes on the same system (true story!). After all, Xcode installation bumps the “global” versions of CoreDevice and CoreSimulator. Hence any bugs in the beta Xcode simulator are visible when you’re using ostensibly stable Xcode versions. So now you are maintaining image versions with and without the pre-release Xcodes. And now you have 2 TB of VM images. On what? A 2 TB MacBook hard drive? That’s the challenge we faced: we need to build, distribute, and store huge images across the fleet of hundreds of machines. Build process Building images is a repeatable process so that we can reliably produce new images when Apple releases new software versions. Building is driven by a script that replicates installation and configuration as a human user would do it (e.g. the build script can run shell commands, click UI buttons or reboot the VM). Wherever possible we stick to using controls designed by Apple to configure the VMs in order to avoid surprising behaviours inconsistent with what a typical local user would be seeing. Naturally, building images is an automated and repeatable process. It is driven by a workflow expressed as a sequence of operations in a YAML file. Operations can be VM control (e.g. reboot), running a shell script or programmatic interaction with the system or setup UI over VNC. Resulting VM images are handed over to Namespace internal Image Registry , in fact the same one that handles Linux and Windows image storage, replication and distribution (covered in the excellent article by Matteo ). Disk images are of course quite different from normal container images: OCI layers are simple tarballs of files, while disks are generally flat arrays of bytes. Very large arrays in fact. And to a large extent they contain empty space: that’s the disk space that would be available to users as free space. Naturally, it would be very wasteful to transfer and store the “empty” data in the registry. So we developed a simple format that allows us to preserve the “sparse-ness” of the images when stored in the registry. Unallocated spans of the image take just a few bytes. And there is another important optimization. Remember the example scenario mentioned in the VM Images section: we have an image of the same system that differs only in addition of an extra Xcode installation. Obviously the latter image is built using the former as a base and most of the bytes are unchanged. Our storage format preserves the “shallow copy” relationship and stores such images as multiple layers: the base layer is shared between them, while subsequent layers only contain the modified blocks. image A image B base layer offset=0 len=3 A B C offset=5 len=1 D BASE LAYER SHARE DELTA LAYER STORED ◀ Back Pause Next ▶ Image A is stored as a base layer of block extents, and its holes take no space. Image B shares that base and stores only a delta: the blocks it changed and a hole where D used to be. Distribution At this point we have the images in an OCI registry now. But of course Virtualization framework cannot start a VM directly using a disk residing in the registry. It needs to have something on the node itself: a VM disk can be backed by either an image file on the local host SSD, or it can route disk I/O requests to a server using Network Block Device (NBD) protocol. The latter would allow us to intelligently serve highly demanded data from a local cache, while conserving on-device space by not storing unneeded blocks. But NBD has the same drawback as userspace networking from above: every I/O operation would incur an IPC roundtrip at minimum, including buffer copying and context switches. You see the same pattern as with networking: a very direct hardwired and fast option and an indirect “software-defined” but disappointingly slow option. At Namespace we value performance a lot, so the choice is clear: we’ll serve the images from the local disk. We need to materialize them from OCI images in the registry on the SSD of every node in the fleet. 500 gig images to hundreds and thousands of nodes. And we need to do it fast. Obviously, every node naively downloading from the central registry was not going to work. With the example numbers we are talking about half a petabyte of traffic transferred within, conservatively, tens of minutes. The registry (and the network fabric) would need to serve terabits per second! The bytes that we are distributing are the same going to every node so the obvious solution is to organize a peer-to-peer delivery of these blobs. Each block only needs to be downloaded from the registry once by some node. Then another node that is close by (by certain metric) can download the block directly from the peer and we have two copies. So two more nodes can pull these bytes and so on. The fleet is exponentially flooded. BitTorrent Obviously, BitTorrent was a heavy inspiration for this design. But unlike BitTorrent, which works in a public network of untrusted peers, we could make different tradeoffs leading to better efficiency and predictability. But that’s a topic for another post. copies 0/8 · registry reads 0 nodes Registry block 0x6ed2 N1 N2 N3 N4 N5 N6 N7 N8 Each block is read from the registry once. Every node that has it passes it to another node, so the number of copies doubles each round. Storage Now the bytes are on the node disk. But remember the storage optimizations we did in the Build Process? With the naive approach of storing the images on disk there are a lot of bytes that are useless: they are either holes or could be shared with another image. Some of you probably know that these are exactly the types of storage optimization techniques that are possible with modern file systems, namely APFS. ZFS Linux users have seen the same features in ZFS. Using these cool features is also pretty easy: open a new file for writing, seek to offset 100G, write a block. And there you just made a file with a large hole in it. Only the block you wrote is allocated on disk, the rest is 100 GB of imaginary zeroes. When reading the file you won’t even notice the holes. The OS will return actual zeros. Creating a sparse file on APFS % truncate -s 1g hole.bin % dd if=/dev/random of=hole.bin bs=4k seek=256k count=256 % ls -lh hole.bin -rw-r--r-- 1 kirill staff 1.0G Sep 29 05:36 hole.bin % du -h hole.bin 1M hole.bin Sharing the blocks is similarly transparent: just use the cp -c mode or clonefile syscall. The new file will share the same disk blocks and essentially not take any space. /dev/disk1 disk usage 0 blocks hole.bin du 0 WRITE CP -C OVERWRITE WRITE B ◀ Back Pause Next ▶ hole.bin allocates only the blocks that were written. cp -c makes clone.bin share those blocks, and writing to the clone allocates only the blocks that change. Writing to the cloned file is also transparent: as soon as you try to overwrite some blocks, these particular blocks will be allocated on the disk, while the shared portion will remain shared. What’s next? The pace at which we are expanding our fleet is increasing and the experience from all the above has transformed into a repeatable process. We know exactly how long it takes to bring a MacBook rack into prod. The rack assembly line is dialed in. DCOps people are trained. Disk images are built and distributed. We can bring whatever number of machines our customers need into the fleet when we need to (well, as long as we can purchase them at all). We can still do better! What if there was a “holy-grail” device to host a shelf of MacBooks, providing power, ethernet and KVM connections over a single USB-C cable? It should be possible, yet there is currently no hardware on the open market that satisfies our requirements. So we are working on something very custom. Or maybe we’ll do another crazy thing? What if we deploy phones to the datacenter? See what the future brings on our X soon! name logo The dev platform for the next 100 billion commits. body_text: Toit v2.0.0 — Toit blog Skip to content Scripting Embedded Docs Project Blog GitHub ← The Toit blog Toit v2.0.0 Celebrating Toit v2.0.0 after more than four years of alpha development. October 31, 2026 · Florian Loitsch After more than four years of alpha development, 2,000+ commits, 500,000+ lines changed, and 200+ alpha releases, Toit v2.0.0 is finally here. Toit began as closed-source software developed by Toitware. It later became an open-source project, and volunteers have continued improving it even after Toitware shut down in 2024. Despite the "alpha" label, Toit has been stable for a long time. Two things kept us from calling it v2.0.0: we still had some breaking changes planned, and there was always another important feature we wanted to include. Recently, we landed a refactoring that lets peripheral APIs accept pin numbers directly instead of requiring gpio.Pin objects. That was the last major breaking change on our list for v2.0.0. As for waiting until all the important features are finished: we have accepted that this moment will never come. Even now, there are open PRs for a formatter, compiler resolution improvements, and support for more architectures, among other major features. Those will follow in future releases. Here are a few highlights since Toit was open-sourced: Broader hardware support, including the Arm-based EC618 and almost all ESP32 variants. A unified toit command and improvements that make Toit a more capable desktop scripting language. A rewritten package manager and a growing package ecosystem. Mixins for sharing implementations across classes. Firmware envelopes, allowing users to customize their firmware without rebuilding the SDK. Compiler and runtime improvements. Significantly better hardware testing. Syntax highlighting for Toit on GitHub. Enjoy! ← All articles Subscribe via RSS Toit contributors. Library reference Packages Releases Blog Source

Why Auto-Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the semantic models you already own. With Auto-Ontology, developers can: Discover. Generate an ontology from database metadata, import existing semantic models, and explore the result as a semantic graph. Ground. Give agents one definition per business concept, mapped across tables and databases. Certify. Review, edit, and certify definitions in the UI or through the API. Validate. Check whether a question is answerable before querying, and return the SQL and the agent's steps with each answer. Expose. Serve context to any agent harness through MCP, agent skills, and a REST API. The usual shortcut is to paste the schema into the agent's context window. Auto-Ontology gives the agent tools over the ontology: Schema in the context window Auto-Ontology tools Tokens Grow with every table and column Only the terms and tables the question touches Meaning Column names; the agent infers the rest Business terms mapped to columns and SQL Joins and measures Improvised per question Resolved relationships and reviewed SQL expressions Unanswerable questions Answered confidently, often wrongly Answerability check, so the agent asks to clarify Evaluation The companion repository, auto-ontology-eval , measures ontology performance on benchmarks and evals. For BIRD, BEAVER, FDABench-Lite, and Wide World Importers, each eval item pairs a question with gold SQL, and a run asks every question of the same model twice: Control. The model gets the database schema in its prompt. Treatment. Auto-Ontology's question-answering agent, the one behind Chat, works from the compiled ontology. A deterministic verifier scores the SQL from each arm by execution match, using each benchmark's official rule where it has one. The report gives the accuracy difference and lists the questions the ontology fixed and the ones it broke. BIRD-Interact, a multi-turn benchmark where the agent asks clarifying questions, runs on its own harness. To run the comparison on BIRD, follow the auto-ontology-eval setup, then run: uv run python main.py --database-name bird Quickstart This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers, Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2, uv , and an NVIDIA API key ( nvapi-... ) from build.nvidia.com . Clone the repository and create .env : git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology cp .env.example .env Then set these values in .env : DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY = nvapi-... AUTH_SECRET = <a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32> APP_URL = http://localhost:3000 POSTGRES_PASSWORD = <a new password> CONNECTION_STRINGS = postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password> PGADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password> Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY . Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set: docker compose up -d --wait postgres git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \ POSTGRES_PASSWORD= ' <the same password> ' \ uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop) Build and start the rest of the stack: docker compose up -d --build Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env . Go to Settings → Semantic Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes. Ask a question in Chat : What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015? The agent resolves revenue , product , and state to terms in the ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it, so you can check the result against the source: Answer: Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines. SQL: SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines FROM sales.invoicelines il JOIN sales.invoices i ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid JOIN warehouse.stockitems si ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid JOIN sales.customers c ON i.customerid = c.customerid JOIN application.cities ct ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll' AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania' AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01' Steps: Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province Validated the filter values against the data, then executed Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve against. An agent connected through MCP checks answerability first and asks you to clarify: You: What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015? Agent: check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend" Agent: I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another source I should connect? If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for localhost:3000 and sign in again. For other setup failures, see the setup skill's troubleshooting guide . How it works Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify it, and the agent answers questions from it. The ontology holds three kinds of definition: Terms. Business concepts such as Customer or Invoice Line , each with a description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them. SQL attributes. Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the same way. Relationships. How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from keys and from the data. Generate. The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source databases: Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the catalog. Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns. Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and suggest SQL attributes from query history. Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval. The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting Order shows its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes: Certify. People make the draft trustworthy: Test with real questions in Chat, or with check_answerable and ask_question over MCP. Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API. Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct. Answer. For each question, the agent: Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names. Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search. Writes SQL from those candidates. Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the SQL when a check fails. Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took. When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's configured (see Predictions ). In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as CSV, or read them as a chart: Auto-Ontology is compatible with Apache Ossie , the open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a converter for Auto-Ontology , which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML. Use Settings → Import / Export , or POST /api/model/import and POST /api/model/export . Component Technology Role Port Frontend Next.js, Better Auth, Prisma Web UI, authentication, public API gateway 3000 Backend FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain Text-to-SQL agent, catalog, ontology APIs 3001 Ingestion service FastAPI (Python 3.12+) Ingestion and semantic compilation 3002 MCP server FastMCP Read-only agent tools over the public API 3003 Postgres + pgvector PostgreSQL 17 Catalog, ontology, app data, vector store 5432 HashiCorp Vault Optional Connection credential storage n/a Keep ports 3001 and 3002 on a private network. FastAPI trusts the user identity the frontend forwards in the x-auto-ontology-user-id header, and the ingestion service's endpoints (ingest, delete, reset, compile) have no authentication of their own. Clients go through the web app on port 3000. Use it from your agent MCP server The MCP server gives any MCP client read-only tools over the ontology. Each user signs in through Auto-Ontology, and every call runs with that user's permissions. Job Tools Readiness check_readiness : can this deployment answer anything at all Terms search_terms , get_term , get_term_columns , get_term_sql_attributes , get_sql_attribute , describe_table Answerability check_answerable : does the ontology cover this question Questions ask_question : the answer, the SQL, and the rows Run the server against your deployment: AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \ uvx --from " git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git#subdirectory=mcp " auto-ontology-mcp Cursor ( ~/.cursor/mcp.json ): { "mcpServers" : { "auto-ontology" : { "url" : " http://localhost:3003/mcp " } } } Claude Desktop ( claude_desktop_config.json ), bridged with mcp-remote : { "mcpServers" : { "auto-ontology" : { "command" : " npx " , "args" : [ " mcp-remote " , " http://localhost:3003/mcp " ] } } } Restart the client after editing its config, then sign in when it prompts. Sign-in, configuration, and troubleshooting are in docs/mcp.md . Agent skills Three skills teach a coding agent to work with Auto-Ontology. Start at AGENTS.md . Skill Covers nvidia-ontology-setup Install, connect sources, compile, prove readiness nvidia-ontology-management Inspect, model, certify, import/export, and publish nvidia-ontology-query Ask questions and validate the SQL, rows, and answer REST API Ask a question with POST /api/chat/completions on the web app's origin. Mint an API token under the user menu → API Tokens . The response is a server-sent event stream: a result event carries the answer, and data: [DONE] ends the stream. curl -N http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions \ -H " x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN " \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"} ' import json import os import requests response = requests . post ( "http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions" , headers = { "x-api-key" : os . environ [ "AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" ]}, json = { "question" : "How many orders shipped last week?" }, stream = True , timeout = 900 , ) response . raise_for_status () for line in response . iter_lines ( decode_unicode = True ): if not line or not line . startswith ( "data:" ): continue payload = line . removeprefix ( "data:" ). strip () if payload == "[DONE]" : break event = json . loads ( payload ) if event [ "type" ] == "result" : print ( event [ "answer" ][ "response" ]) print ( event [ "answer" ][ "sql_code" ]) elif event [ "type" ] == "error" : raise RuntimeError ( event [ "message" ]) Event types, multi-turn conversations, and the gateway trust boundary are in docs/conversation-api.md . Every other operation is in the OpenAPI spec . Connectors, models, and predictions Sources Auto-Ontology connects to ten engines: PostgreSQL MySQL Databricks Snowflake ClickHouse Trino Apache Kyuubi HeavyDB DuckDB SQLite Add connections under Settings → Connections , or list them in CONNECTION_STRINGS . DuckDB and SQLite are connection-string only. See docs/connections.md for URL schemes, scoping, and credential storage. Models Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an nvapi- key, each defaults to an NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com : Role Default model What it does REASONING nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b Builds the ontology (terms, relationships, SQL attributes), writes each answer's SQL and explanation, and grades answerability NON_REASONING nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b Runs the agent's faster steps: question intent, entity extraction, candidate selection, and SQL checks and repair EMBED nvidia/nemotron-3.5-embed-1b Indexes tables, columns, terms, and SQL attributes in pgvector, and matches each question to them RERANK nvidia/nemotron-3.5-rerank-8b Ranks candidate tables when compilation builds bridge-table SQL attributes To use self-hosted NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set <ROLE>_ENDPOINT , <ROLE>_API_KEY , and <ROLE>_MODEL . Any field you leave unset falls back to DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD> , so the simplest setup fills in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and overrides only what differs. Use models that support structured output, and keep the embedding model the same for ingestion and queries. .env.example documents every variable. Predictions Set KUMO_RFM_API_KEY and the agent routes predictive questions to KumoRFM. KumoRFM is a hosted service: to answer, the agent uploads the connected tables to it, capped by KUMO_MAX_TABLES (20 by default) and KUMO_MAX_ROWS_PER_TABLE (unlimited unless set). Review what that sends, and complete your organization's data review, before you enable it. Integrate with us To integrate an agent platform, application, or storage provider with Auto-Ontology, open an integration request . The Auto-Ontology team maintains the code and doesn't accept external pull requests. Integration requests and bug reports are welcome as issues. Report security vulnerabilities through SECURITY.md . Maintainer workflow is in CONTRIBUTING.md . title: Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws
body_text: Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws - Ars Technica Skip to content Ars Technica home Sections Forum Subscribe Search AI Biz & IT Cars Culture Gaming Health Policy Science Security Space Tech Feature Reviews AI Biz & IT Cars Culture Gaming Health Policy Science Security Space Tech Forum Subscribe Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Pin to story Theme HyperLight Day & Night Dark System Search Sign In Sign in dialog... Sign in Criminal charges for Kalshi Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws Charges filed as Trump admin tries to save Kalshi from Utah’s total ban on gambling. Jon Brodkin – Oct 29, 2026 1:21 pm | 240 Credit: Getty Images | Martin Lelievre Credit: Getty Images | Martin Lelievre Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets. Meanwhile, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed criminal charges in a state court against Kalshi and its founders on Wednesday. The attorney general’s office provided us with court filings listing charges against KalshiEX, LLC , Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour , and Kalshi co-founder and COO Luana Lopes Lara . The company and two co-founders each face 13 felony charges and one misdemeanor for violating gambling laws. The charges are based on sports bets offered on Kalshi between September 13 and September 24. “The state did not issue arrest warrants for Monsour and Lopes Lara. Instead, they have been issued summons to respond to the charges in Third District Court in Salt Lake County,” The Salt Lake Tribune wrote . The Utah News Dispatch quoted a Kalshi statement vowing to fight the charges. “This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” the statement said, referring to similar charges the company beat in Arizona in May. Utah, which prohibits gambling, filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events. “Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.” Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Trump admin claims sole authority The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said on Tuesday . “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.” If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products , including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC. The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filed lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases. “Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.” The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with by courts throughout the US are whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws. US sues in same court where Utah beat Kalshi The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor. Kalshi sued Utah in February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market. In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelby wrote , “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.” Shelby determined the text of US law makes it clear that state regulation is not forbidden. US law states that CFTC jurisdiction does not “supersede or limit the jurisdiction conferred on courts of the United States or any State,” and “explicitly provides for State regulation of its gaming laws in all but a few specified cases,” he wrote. “Congress is aware that some States permit gambling while others do not, and the CEA explicitly provides for State jurisdiction,” Shelby wrote. Most states in US want Supreme Court to rule Kalshi is now appealing its loss to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit but was unable to obtain an injunction preventing enforcement of the state gambling ban while that litigation continues. On September 8, Tenth Circuit judges denied Kalshi’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal. Utah filed its lawsuit seeking a shutdown of Kalshi about six weeks later. The CFTC lawsuit against Utah makes arguments similar to the ones already rejected by the district court, although some other courts have ruled otherwise. “Utah is not the first State that has attempted to invade the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over swaps,” the CFTC lawsuit said. “Already, several federal courts—including the Third Circuit—have swiftly responded by issuing or affirming temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions barring the States from enforcing their gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges that offer sports-related or other event contracts.” The Third Circuit appeals court ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. But Kalshi lost similar cases in the Sixth Circuit and Ninth Circuit in rulings that went in favor of Ohio, Tennessee, and Nevada. Because circuit appeals courts are divided on the issue, it is likely that the Supreme Court will take up the case and determine whether states can apply their gambling laws to prediction markets. New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Court to resolve the circuit split, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s petition. This article was originally published on October 28 at 3:30 pm ET and updated on October 29 with information about the felony charges filed against Kalshi and its co-founders . title: Resisting Cognitive Surrender
body_text: knlb.dev | Resisting Cognitive Surrender Working Notes: a commonplace notebook for recording & exploring ideas. Home . Site Map . Subscribe . More at expLog . — Kunal Resisting Cognitive Surrender sitemap / essays Details updates - 2026-10-25 A quick round of editing with Codex - 2026-10-31 Tightening my arguments and reorganizing - 2026-11-01 First final version, upgraded this to an essay rss true updated 2026-11-01 Contents Cognitive surrender is seductive Why not surrender? Solutions There are still tradeoffs Choose your vibe limit & triage Watch out for automation bias Force yourself into the loop Force comprehensibility When you do decide to delegate Good design is a force multiplier Additional reading Related notes/exploratory_programming notes/how/engineer/not_engineer notes/tools_for_thought notes/how/strategy notes/procrastination notes/positive_intelligence notes/software_design notes/how/engineer/planning notes/writing/approaches notes/tech_talks_ideas This particular note is around exploring cognitive surrender : uncritically accepting whatever agents output without actually thinking , exploring or considering alternatives. Working this way is extremely fast, not particularly taxing, and unsurprisingly seductive. And yet I find myself repeatedly questioning if this is actually a good way to apply agents: often enough I find myself making suboptimal decisions, accruing technical debt and reducing my familiarity with the system I’m working on instead of improving it. As we collectively rethink how we work I’ve been finding it useful to read and share other people’s workflows, and consciously write about and examine my own. This particular post focuses on finding the right balance of trust while working with agents. Cognitive surrender is seductive One of the virtues of being a great programmer is to be lazy . After more than a decade of training myself to look for the shortest and simplest path it’s rather attractive to be able to simply hand over the problem. If I can spin up a software factory, why wouldn’t I? There’s also a lot of peer pressure (or game theory) at work: if any of my colleagues have seemingly surrendered, then I’m only going to look worse if I spend too much time trying to do silly things like understanding what I’m working on. And, of course , while everyone else is a slop-cannon generating code faster than they can read it I can build a meticulously designed software factory manufacturing perfect designs. The sheer volume of work also appears remarkably productive – we’ve all talked about just how many more PRs we ship every day. This tends to get compounded by the agents’ expressed confidence & conviction. Perhaps an inadvertent consequence of RLHF, but models tend to be astonishingly confident in what they recommend (and perhaps even more blasé while admitting they made a mistake). This makes it too easy to take their answers at face value, with whatever social programming I seem to have evolved with. OSS projects – particularly those facing time pressure – seem to accrue tremendous complexity quickly, to the point that it feels like the only way to interact with a project in any sane time frame is by heavily relying on agents to navigate and modify and test the code. This is also a self-reinforcing feedback loop: broken windows multiply rapidly with agents on the loose. [1] Technical debt and incidental complexity have a fairly attenuated feedback loop: complexity introduced by slop doesn’t bite immediately; it’s far more subtle and compounds over time when I’m not paying attention. Beyond all of that, I have to mention the hype cycle. We all should be skipping Netflix to watch talks by Anthropic engineers on making loops (or the agentic workflow du jour ). [2] Why not surrender? It’s not entirely obvious that it’s a bad idea to surrender: if it’s easier and better , then why not take that path? So far, my personal answer is that I need to take the easier path consciously and intentionally, with enough effort to mitigate downsides. Part of what makes me deeply uncomfortable is suffering from a form of Gell-Mann amnesia while working with agents. When I have expertise and the overall design direction I can generally simplify the output significantly, controlling for complexity. When I don’t they seem to be the smartest engineers in existence – far beyond the more squishy, organic variety – and all I can do is follow in awe. And then the agent gets stuck creating a directory and I have to reset all my assumptions. For the current state of the art (October 2026) I generally find maximal use of agents leads to a significant explosion in complexity: something that mostly works, with extremely surprising edge cases and bugs. These are generally the projects with hundreds of thousands of lines of code shipped rapidly, breaking the scale supported by most software development tools, so you also need to revisit those – and this compounds rapidly. I have a strong aversion to incidental complexity, and generally refuse to build, maintain or extend it: it’s fine for a proof-of-concept, but it must end there. For systems that need to keep working, steering the design aggressively towards simplicity and modularity is what lets me build something I can actually operate (with and without agents). As models continue to improve rapidly, I expect the previous argument to go away as the models learn and can express a broader sense of engineering taste, good design and quality. The other reason – which I unfortunately expect to persist – is that my personal understanding and mechanical sympathy for systems I maintain erode extremely rapidly, or never get a chance to develop. In the early days when I would build things by hand I’d be able to quickly diagnose any bug or misbehavior based on my familiarity with building and maintaining the code: the more I rely on agents, the more my only option is to spin up one more session and hope; and the automated fix then further reduces my understanding in a self-reinforcing loop. Without context, I no longer have much meaningful judgement and can’t engage – or handle it in context. The Ironies of Automation (1983) is referred to often in articles similar to this one. I’d recommend directly reading the paper if you haven’t: it’s fully relevant to the decisions we have to make today. The paper warns that it becomes even harder to deal with tasks an agent fails at because we never manage to get any practice with the easier tasks; nor do we get a chance to internalize what a system feels like under standard operating circumstances. At the end of the day, I’m responsible and accountable for what I build, not the agents. Surrendering agency and not thinking basically makes me accountable without any meaningful ownership. There’s also the small matter of pride in the quality of my work. [3] Solutions The sombre opening shouldn’t lead you to believe that I’m not excited about the sheer potential unlocked by AI, and the opportunities to build things that I would never have been able to without it. It’s more about resetting expectations, explicitly working through the tradeoffs involved and choosing which ones are acceptable. And finding ways to maintain the quality and craftsmanship I care about. There are still tradeoffs The first step for me has been to internalize that I can’t truly have my cake and eat it: I can go terribly, inhumanly fast at building things but I need to accept that there’s no way to retain the mechanical sympathy, depth and confidence I used to have without putting in the effort. Time that used to be only counted as building a system also involved comprehension ; agents can drive the time to build to zero but the next bottleneck – comprehension – hasn’t moved much so far. The hype cycle occasionally can make it hard to communicate this explicitly: a lot of the communication around agentic loops tends to assume that there are no downsides whatsoever. Choose your vibe limit & triage Several months ago I defined my vibe limit as the complexity of the change I can make with sufficient confidence using agents. I like the risk/complexity curve enough to post it again: The next step is figuring out where I land: there are several projects where good enough is fine, or the problem is sufficiently sandboxed that I’m happy to live with whatever the agents generated. On the other hand, if the system is important, fragile, can’t be sanity checked easily or isn’t particularly well isolated I need to directly spend my time. Aggressive prioritization, triage, and constantly recalibrating myself become really important in this ecosystem: I should explicitly choose where to surrender agency and where to spend my time (not unlike leading a team, except the pace is much faster). Constantly reviewing my predictions and the outcomes helps a lot in recalibrating, particularly with new model drops. Watch out for automation bias I also find myself needing to be much more mindful while working. A warning sign I watch out for these days is if I find myself repeatedly tapping “yes, continue” in a session. At that point either I should figure out what it would take to completely delegate the problem to Claude instead of trying to micro-manage the agent – or realize that I stopped thinking and I need to check the decisions being made. Completely delegating the problem generally means building a better sandbox or feedback loop, or figuring out ways to be able to sanity check much more easily before shipping to production. Alternatively, if I need to engage much more deeply I’ll use some of the other tactics described below. Force yourself into the loop The premise of augmenting myself by working in the loop with powerful thinking machines was a large part of my decision to join my current company. This generally comes down to directions you can give the model to reduce the size of the steps it takes, or explicitly choosing to drive instead of passively observing. For projects I deeply care about, choosing to drive instead of letting the model drive is one way to intervene in every single decision. It’s much slower to type things out, but it does force me to engage with every decision and gives me an opportunity to override it. In fact, for this post I’m using a Codex session to edit: help me tighten the post, point out the small typos, punctuation errors, or half-finished sentences that tend to embarrass me after I explicitly share a post publicly – but I make all changes by hand . In the AGENTS.md for the notebook: Never edit files directly, always wait for the author to request or confirm changes, or let him make the edits directly. This is reminiscent of how I used to work with Stack Overflow: never copy-paste code; instead write it out explicitly while cross-checking with documentation. Either I’d learn and internalize something new or I’d realize the Stack Overflow answer was suboptimal or outdated. Force comprehensibility We don’t need to limit ourselves to existing interfaces anymore: with agents it’s also possible to have them build a tremendous amount of scaffolding to support comprehension and make changes in ways that are digestible. Often enough for larger, complex stacks I have the agents build me a custom view for the Pull Request with 4 columns: the standard 2 for the diff, a 3rd column with running commentary from the agent on why it made a particular change and finally the 4th column as a place for me to add comments and directions. Getting the agents to make stacks of changes with the explicit direction to “Make the change easy, then make the easy change” works really well. I used to spend a lot of time trying to make my diffs easily reviewable to respect the reviewers’ time – now I can ask the agents to do the same for me. It’s also very valuable to dive into actual execution with a debugger (or have an agent manipulate the debugger on your behalf) till you get a deep sense of how things are flowing through the program, with the confidence that this is the real execution path. Another example is to make harnesses explain what they’re doing: I’ve built several variations of command-line helpers that transparently fit into my shell sessions ( x being the last public version). In my most recent iteration, I explicitly ask the model to explain any obscure flags and commands used so that I can learn as I go. When you do decide to delegate Sometimes, it does make sense to hand over the problem to an agent: it could be too big, not valuable enough, time could be too short, or you just want to get a first prototype out to explore a problem end-to-end. This one is probably an essay by itself: adapting old-school best practices when you have infinitely fast stochastic intelligence on top. The idea here is to reduce the risk in making changes, flattening the vibe-limit curve and making it possible to make bigger changes safely. Beyond giving the agent some means to verify itself against the goal you’re aiming for, I find it very useful to: Observability : Invest heavily in observability, both black-box and white-box, and make sure to keep a direct handle on the metrics instead of solely relying on the agents’ view. As a habit I prefer to triangulate onto a behavior with multiple sources of metrics, and that becomes even more important with systems rapidly becoming opaque. Non-functional requirements : Don’t forget to observe resource utilization and other non-functional requirements: these can be canaries for unexpected behavior. Deterministic validation : Build mechanical straitjackets for the model: have held-out pieces of code or deterministic tools for validation and observations as a hold-out against the model misunderstanding or glitching. Shadow Traffic : Make it possible and cheap to run a deployed candidate against shadow traffic with no side effects: keep it as similar to production as possible, and this can be the final gate to prevent surprises. Style guides : Give the model a style guide based on your existing code and work. I’ve found Claude’s output far more to my taste after having the models generate a style guide based on all the code and blog posts I’ve written in the past. Fast deploys : An often maligned motto at Facebook used to be Move Fast & Break Things : that, too, is an intentional tradeoff to make. If you can’t be sure of quality, make it very easy to deploy code as well – so changes can be shipped and reverted extremely rapidly. Rethink what’s possible : It’s surprisingly easy to write and rewrite systems from scratch rapidly as you learn. Build to throw, evaluate, and repeat to get something knocked into great shape – I’ve built projects in multiple iterations, giving the agent the previous iteration and its limitations as initial context and constantly finding myself able to deeply increase the quality. This doesn’t work as well when you’re punishing your code reviewers though, so make sure to align with your team, or simply don’t get the first several iterations reviewed. Good design is a force multiplier In Notes on the Synthesis of Form Christopher Alexander has a wonderful example demonstrating the value of decomposition – or building a lightly coupled, cohesive system to be able to succeed quickly. No complex adaptive system will succeed in adapting in a reasonable amount of time unless the adaptation can proceed subsystem by subsystem, each subsystem relatively independent of the others. Whether agents or humans are doing the work, a good design makes the system much easier to understand, iterate on, validate and extend. As you learn the limitations of the design, you also now have the ability to redo it much more rapidly than ever before. Regardless of how much depth you decide to maintain in your projects, I’d make sure the broader structure continues to make sense. Additional reading There are several interesting articles, talks and books that are relevant: Addy Osmani with several additional techniques Guy Levi recommending leaning into critical thinking Cory Doctorow talking about handling being forced to use AI Stuart Halloway emphasizing that AI is automation, and the importance of friction to build metis . Elizabeth, SigNoz on skills atrophying. Ricard Solé et al. on LLMs as a cognitive virus, modeling the interaction and consequences of cognitive offloading. I’m curious if you have any other recommendations around effectively leveraging agents without losing context – I’d love to hear about additional experiments to try or workflows to adopt! Particularly if you’ve successfully recovered projects that collapsed into slop. Discuss on Hacker News . I have constantly been expecting more software to fail under the weight of its own complexity. One of my hot takes is that this hasn’t happened at the scale and magnitude I expect yet because agents became smarter fast enough to keep up with the debt introduced by the previous generation. ↩︎ You’ll pry my weekly indulgence in The Great British Baking Show from my cold, dead hands. ↩︎ You could argue that this is a very “Individual Contributor” approach to building things, and that managers deal with this all the time. I’ll quote Andrew Grove on management: “delegation without follow-through is abdication” – you still need to engage to get the outcome you need. ↩︎

body_text: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise 813 points by aarushyadav 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 384 comments Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) ( https://subvocal.company/ ). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech. Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI (Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.) Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV... We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology. We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work: - Signal changes due to sweat - Electrical interference - Placement variability - Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!! So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text. Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc... Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C... This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas. That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data. So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration). We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well. Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases. For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Not everyone with signs of the disease in the brain develops symptoms. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Not all people with signs of CTE go on to experience cognitive decline, and some people may never experience symptoms at all. James Black / Icon Sportswire via Getty Share Add NBC News to Google Oct. 28, 2026, 11:01 AM EDT By Kaitlin Sullivan An estimated 75% of professional football players who died over a 15-year span had signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a study published Wednesday found. It’s the highest estimate to date. Most recently, a study published in August by the same group estimated that one-quarter of NFL players who died in a five-year span had CTE. The new study, published in JAMA Network Open , put the figure at three times higher. Not all people with signs of CTE in the brain go on to experience cognitive decline or dementia, and some people may never experience symptoms at all. A smaller proportion of the former players in the analysis were estimated to have dementia, about 27%, the study found. The results were surprising, said study leader Yorghos Tripodis, the director of statistics and data management at the Boston University Alzheimer’s Disease and CTE Center. Boston University houses the UNITE Brain Bank , which studies the effects of repetitive head trauma in donated brains, including the brains of athletes, military personnel and others. “I had to double-check the numbers,” Tripodis said. Still, he said, the number is a best guess. “Right now we don’t know how to diagnose CTE when people are alive, so we are trying to estimate.” In an emailed statement, an NFL spokesperson said, in part, that the league “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.” Repeated blows and bias When a person’s head jolts during an impact, the brain — which is suspended in fluid inside the skull — can slam into the skull or twist, said Dr. Julian Bailes, chair of the neurosurgery department at Endeavor Health in the Chicago area. Each blow is an opportunity for proteins called tau to build up in the brain. “If that happens over and over again, that damage accrues,” said Bailes, who wasn’t involved with the new research. The disease can affect parts of the brain involved with regulating behavior and emotions , which can lead to memory loss, depression, violent mood swings and other symptoms. Those symptoms can also be linked to other illnesses. Although CTE can cause symptoms similar to those of other neurodegenerative diseases, such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, the signature it leaves on the brain is unique, Bailes said. One huge hurdle in studying the prevalence of CTE is that the microscopic changes don’t show up on brain scans. That means the condition can be diagnosed only during an autopsy. Past research has been criticized for bias, since people with cognitive decline and their families are much likelier to either donate their brains to brain banks after they die or ask for autopsies — a previous study by Boston University researchers found that 99% of the brains donated to research by former NFL players had signs of CTE. In the new study, Tripodis and his team tried to remove as much of that bias as possible to determine a more accurate estimate of CTE rates in former NFL players. They combined data from the UNITE Brain Bank with national death records of other former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023. In total, the researchers looked at data from 396 donated brains, plus information from 1,966 other deceased former NFL players. They factored in the ages of death along with estimated rates of mild cognitive impairment and dementia in former NFL players older than 50. About 93% of the donated brains had signs of CTE, which shows up as structural damage in the brain. The research team calculated that the families of players with symptoms of cognitive decline were about five times likelier to donate brains than the families of players without symptoms and then performed a statistical analysis to correct for that bias. In comparison, only about 1% of brains donated to banks in the U.S., Austria and Brazil have signs of the disease, the researchers said. But plenty of people with signs of CTE never develop symptoms, Tripodis said. The researchers estimated that 27% of the 2,360 players studied had dementia. The dementia “can be from all causes,” Tripodis said. “But it is very likely that in this specific population that CTE is causing dementia.” Reducing impacts Until doctors figure out a way to diagnose CTE while people are still alive, any studies quantifying how many people have the condition will be estimates, said Dr. Jim Kelly, a professor emeritus of neurology at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “These are all estimates. They had no autopsies on five times as many players who died as they did have autopsies for,” said Kelly, who wasn’t involved in the research. Some of the autopsies may also have revealed just one or a couple of lesions associated with CTE, “and it seems unlikely that that would lead to anything in terms of a behavior change or dementia,” he said. Those are difficult studies to do, Bailes agreed. They seek to determine “how many people out there have a condition when not all of them are symptomatic,” he said, adding that the findings are a call for more research into diagnosing CTE in people who are still living. “If you can’t tell if someone has a certain disease until they’re dead, you really can’t help them,” he said. In the meantime, prevention is key, Tripodis said: “If you reduce the number of brain injuries, brain impacts, you substantially decrease the risk.” The NFL has already implemented measures to try to reduce the number of high-impact hits players face. They include redesigned helmets — such as the Guardian Cap — and the dynamic kickoff rule , which leads to lower collision speeds. WAV+CUE，或使用即时刻录功能直接写入空白盘片。 即时刻录为实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。 功能 光盘数据生成 CD 支持 ：支持任何 CD 。您可导出带格式头的 WAV 音轨及配套 CUE，兼容 cdrecord, ImgBurn等刻录软件；也允许导出 RAW 音轨。详见 CD 刻录兼容说明 。 DVD 支持 ：支持任何 DVD。您可导出 ISO 镜像。 蓝光支持 ：支持任何单层 BD-R 25 GB，支持纯绘图与 UDF 2.01 文件。详见 ADDING_BLURAY.md 。 随盘文件 ：CD／DVD／蓝光可在设计页直接选择要保存的文件夹及内圈／外圈位置，也可在导出页调整；设置随工程保存。 文件区域预览 ：混合盘的设计投影和成品读回用黄色标出文件区（含文件系统）。 介质灰度方案 ：CD 与 DVD 均使用黑白二阶，CD 使用 0D / AA ，DVD 扰码域使用 A5 / 92 。详见 PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md 。 灰度抖动工具 ：独立程序也可将原图处理为 0/255 黑白二阶 PNG；支持打开或拖入原图、并排预览及无损 PNG 导出。详见 使用与构建说明 。 盘片预设 ：内置数个品牌的光盘参数，覆盖 CD／DVD／BD。您也可将自己标定好的数据贡献给我们，详见 预设维护说明 。 辅助标定 Disc Image Studio 提供了一套智能且精准的辅助标定流程，相较人工肉眼识别标定，辅助标定算法将可确定的盘面物理数据精确度从 10 -6 提升到了 10 -14 。校准前采用恒定轨距，十字线的径向线条出现明显弯曲；使用辅助标定得到的三次轨距参数重新生成并刻录后，线条更接近径向直线。 校准前 · 恒定轨距 校准后 · 三次轨距 P20261004-133519.jpg P20261004-135416.jpg 流程与参数说明见 辅助标定说明 。 刻录 镜像文件输出 ：您可以导出完整 ISO / RAW 文件并使用合适的刻录软件手动刻录。 即时流式刻录（实验性） ：CD、DVD 与 BD-R 边生成边刻录，不保存完整镜像；BD-R 走 MMC 顺序写入。 不要使用非空白介质！ 系统与设备要求 桌面版需要 Windows 10 2004（2004/20H1，19041）及以上，或 Windows 11。 构建：.NET 10 SDK（ global.json 锁定 10.0.x）；自行构建的非自包含 GUI 需要 .NET 10 Windows 桌面运行时。Release EXE 已包含运行时，无需另行安装 .NET。 “即时刻录”功能需要一台 Windows 可识别的 CD / DVD / BD 刻录机与空白盘片；BD-R 需要支持顺序写入的单层空白盘。 构建与运行 dotnet build DiscImageStudio.slnx -- configuration Release dotnet run -- project src / DiscImageStudio.App -- configuration Release 构建回归检查： dotnet run -- project src / DvdImageSolver -- configuration Release -- selftest dotnet run -- project tests / DiscImageStudio.ArchitectureTests -- configuration Release 版本规则、CI 生成 EXE、Release 草稿检查、MSIX 打包与签名流程见 发布指南 。 命令行 Linux（glibc）可选 linux-x64 或 linux-arm64 。Apple Silicon Mac 选 osx-arm64 ，Intel Mac 选 osx-x64 。CLI 在本地生成镜像，实际写盘可交给支持相应镜像或音轨的刻录软件。 使用 .NET 10 SDK 从源码运行 CLI dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.Cli -c Release -- --help CLI 可读取 PNG、JPEG、BMP 和 GIF，使用动画图片的第一帧。下面的例子用两扇区音轨验证安装，同时生成配套 CUE。 ./disc-image-studio cd-generate --input picture.png --output sample.wav --sectors 2 命令 说明 solve 使用固定快速纹理映射（CW 方向）生成 DVD 镜像，黑白纹理可选抖动混合 encode 将单个 DVD ECC 块编码为 NRZI 通道电平 calibrate 标定投影：按生成几何从 DVD 源图片取样，按实测几何投到盘面 simulate 按实测半径对生成的 DVD ISO 做读回模拟 selftest 运行 DVD 引擎的确定性回归自检 cd-generate 无随盘文件时生成 WAV + CUE / RAW 音轨；指定 --data-dir 时生成 CD 数据盘 ISO cd-preview-warp 标定投影：按实测几何投影 CD 源图片 cd-preview-track 按标定几何渲染已有的 WAV 或 RAW CD-DA 音轨（读回模拟） bd-generate 生成完整 BD-R ISO，并写出 <iso>.json sidecar bd-info / bd-probe / bd-encode 导出 BD 参数、原始负载探针或单个 ECC 簇诊断 各命令的完整参数见对应文档。 源码结构 src/DiscImageStudio.Cli/ Linux 和 macOS 离线命令行入口 src/DiscImageStudio.ImageIO/ WIC 和跨平台图像编解码 src/DiscImageStudio.Core/ 介质无关的模块契约、工程/预设模型、任务与命令目录 src/DiscImageStudio.Imaging/ CD/DVD/BD 共用的图片预处理与抖动辅助 src/DiscImageStudio.Burning/ Windows IMAPI2 设备枚举、流缓冲与安全刻录层 src/DiscImageStudio.Cd/ CD-DA 生成核心与 CD 模块 src/DiscImageStudio.Dvd/ DVD 引擎适配模块 src/DiscImageStudio.BluRay/ BD-R 几何、17PP/ECC、3T/6T 映射、流式生成与 ISO src/DiscImageStudio.Iso/ UDF 2.01 / ISO9660 写入器 src/DiscImageStudio.App/ WPF GUI、统一命令行与商店资源 src/DvdImageSolver/ 保持隔离的 DVD 编码/求解引擎 tests/ 无第三方测试框架的架构回归测试 packaging/ MSIX 清单与打包脚本 tools/ 独立辅助工具与资产生成脚本 docs/ 架构、引擎、预设、发布等文档 文档 文档 内容 ARCHITECTURE.md 模块抽象、层间边界与扩展规则 LOCALIZATION.md 界面语言配置、系统语言回退与翻译资源维护 DVD_ENGINE.md DVD NRZI 图像约束求解器的约定、编码链与自检覆盖 CD_AUDIO_COMPATIBILITY.md CD 音轨格式、字节序与重影排查 ADDING_BLURAY.md 蓝光模块的物理模型、生成/刻录链路与扩展点 DISC_PRESETS.md 可编辑盘片预设的分层 JSON 格式与合并规则 CALIBRATION.md 照片矫正（框选盘片实体最外缘与中心孔边缘）、曲线标定与 DVD 三次轨距拟合 PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md CD / DVD 生成物理模型复核 VALIDATION.md 各轮构建、回归与实盘测试的本地验证记录 RELEASING.md GitHub Release、MSIX 打包、签名测试与商店提交流程 CHANGELOG.md 版本变更记录 参考标准 Disc Image Studio 的实现与物理模型主要参考以下规范： 介质 标准与版本 本项目采用的范围 CD-R ECMA-394，第 1 版，2010 年 12 月 — Recordable Compact Disc Systems CD-R Multi-Speed （ 官方 PDF ） CD-R 介质、多速录制及 CD-DA 兼容关系；本项目生成 CD-DA 音轨。 DVD 公共格式 / DVD-ROM ECMA-267，第 3 版，2001 年 4 月 — 120 mm DVD – Read-only disk （ 官方 PDF ） DVD 数据帧、ECC、EFMPlus 编码及附录 G 转换表；可记录盘的介质规则另参考 ECMA-359。 DVD-R ECMA-359，第 1 版，2004 年 12 月 — 80 mm (1,46 Gbytes per side) and 120 mm (4,70 Gbytes per side) DVD Recordable Disk (DVD-R) （ 官方 PDF ） 单层 DVD-R 的几何、扇区、纠错和编码；标准包含单面及双面介质，双面不等于双层。 BD-R ISO/IEC 30190:2021，第 3 版，2021 年 1 月 — 120 mm 单层（25.0 GB）及双层（50.0 GB）可记录 BD 的信息交换与存储规范 实验模式采用单层 25 GB 的轨道、扇区布局、纠错和编码；目前不支持双层盘。 CD 公共编码部分还参考了 ECMA-130，第 2 版（CD-ROM，1996） 。 刻录与介质安全须知 Disc Image Studio 不安装驱动或服务；“即时刻录”功能使用了 Windows 自带的 IMAPI2，拒绝非空白介质。 “即时刻录”功能已有部分实盘反馈，对不同设备、介质与刻录入口的验证覆盖仍有限，属于实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。刻录中断、断电或生成速度不足仍可能使盘片报废！ 实际可见效果取决于盘片、刻录机、固件与写入策略。 混合文件夹会在开始刻录前扫描目录并固定布局；期间源文件大小改变会安全终止任务，已开始写入的盘片仍可能报废。 BD-R 顺序写入不提供备用区重映射；中断后同一盘片通常不能继续写入。 隐私与安全 Disc Image Studio 不联网、不上传文件、不收集遥测，详见 隐私政策 。 发现安全问题请不要在公开 Issue 中披露，按 安全政策 使用 GitHub 私密报告。 贡献 欢迎报告问题与提交代码。开发环境搭建、模块边界规则、测试要求与 Pull Request 流程见 贡献指南 。 许可证 项目采用 GNU GPL v3.0 or later （ GPL-3.0-or-later ）。CD 交织实现包含从 CDImage 移植并修改的代码，整体分发沿用兼容的 GPL 授权；分发二进制或修改版时须遵守对应源代码等要求。第三方字体与组件遵循各自许可证，详见 授权说明 和 第三方声明 ；应用"关于"页也可离线查看完整文本。 致谢 感谢 arduinocelentano 的 CDImage 项目 ，它展示了通过生成 CD 音轨在盘面形成可见图像的方法。本项目的 CD 交织实现由其相关代码移植并继续修改，CD 盘面绘图思路也受其启发。CDImage 原作者及贡献者的工作为本项目提供了重要基础。 Star History About No description,
