title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
body_text: HackerTube – karpathy karpathy Home Blog HackerTube 31 Oct, 2026 It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org ! Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews , filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila! HackerTube: Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 EDIT : A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.   Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

title: If you love a website, back it up
body_text: If you love a website, back it up - The Future Is Now The Future Is Now RSS Blog Archives If you love a website, back it up Oct 29 th , 2026 4:21 pm This story starts with a little tragedy. See, Iâve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. Thereâs websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and thereâs something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes. There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken . Itâs about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea. 1 The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads. I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didnât. This post is here to beg you to do what I didnât think to, and to teach you how. You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe itâs something they couldnât do. Itâs something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But thatâs not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can , but should ! Donât just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you donât want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up! All of the tools Iâll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC 2 . You donât have to worry about any of the technical details 3 , but Iâm telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post: You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. Itâs an entire website right in a post! (And if you donât trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose âdownload archiveâ, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!) By the way, for disclosure: the tools Iâm going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but thatâs not because theyâll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving. Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension By far the easiest personal web archiving tool is the ArchiveWeb.page browser extension for Chrome. This doesnât take much in the way of setup or technical skills, and it works for anything: a single page, an entire website, a social media post or profile. So long as you can see it in a web browser, you can save it. All you really need to do is: Install the browser extension . Visit the first page you want to archive. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click âStart Archivingâ. If your page has any interactive elements, click on those to make sure all their data loads. Visit any other pages you want captured in the same collection and let the extension grab them. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click âStop Archivingâ. Youâre done! You just archived a web page! Now that itâs all saved, you can preview it and see how it went by clicking the extensionâs icon and then the home icon to open the extension dashboard. From there, you can click on your archiving session to preview the pages you archived, load them in browser, and see if they work. (Iâll go into more details on how you can look at web archives and share them with others later in this post.) Option 2 - archiveweb.page app If you donât want to install a browser extension, or you donât have Chrome installed, you can also grab the standalone archiveweb.page app . This is basically the same thing as the browser extension above, it just has its own web browser built in. It also opens straight to the menu that lets you browse your web archives, so itâs a handy way to look at your web archives locally. Pretty much everything else I described above applies. Option 3 - Browsertrix The above options are great for single pages or sites that are small enough for you to browse manually. But if youâve got a webpage thatâs big enough that itâs going to be annoying visiting all of the pages by hand, you probably want to look at a web crawler tool for web archiving. There are a bunch of options out there, but the easiest to use as an individual is probably Browsertrix . A web crawler is basically an automation tool built around a web browser; you provide instructions on what page to start from and what pages it should visit, and it will go ahead and click links to automatically find pages so that it can archive the page as completely as possible. The web archive I embedded above was done using Browsertrix on pretty close to its default settings: I just told it I wanted to do a site crawl for the entire domain https://teapuppies.mistys-internet.website , and it worked it out from there: But, depending, on what youâre looking for, it has options which can be customized to narrow down what content it archives. For example, if you decided you only want pages for the episodes, you could tell it to only capture anything at the /episodes/ section of the website: Or even just a single page and anything that page links to: There are a lot more options than I can go into in a quick overview - itâs a comprehensive tool with a lot of options. But if youâre looking to archive a whole website, or a complete social media profile, Iâd recommend giving it a try. Unlike the other tools, which you mainly run on your own computer, Browsertrix is primarily a web app. Itâs also the only paid tool in this post - thereâs a seven day trial, but after that you do have to pay per use. Since itâs open source, though, technically inclined users can run their own copies on their computer or deploy a copy somewhere if they like. Viewing your archived webpage Once youâve actually backed the site up, you can replay it to use it in your browser just like a live webpage. Itâs kind of like having your own private version of the wayback machine. You can test it out yourself for your own private use using the interface built into the version of archiveweb.page you used, but if you want to share it with someone else you have a few options. If you want to share it with someone privately, you can send them the WARC/WACZ file and let them load it into the ArchiveWeb.page app or the ReplayWeb.page website. If you want to share it with the world, though, you can set up a website with your web archive on it. This post is using the ReplayWeb.page embedded viewer, which is open source and can be embedded inside any other web page you want. You donât have run any kind of app on your server to do this; as long as you have the ability to upload the archive and a little bit of JavaScript, you can easily add a copy of the replay interface into any web page or blog post. Preserving the data once you have it Since everything you backed up is bundled inside a single WACZ file, itâs really easy to keep safe - or share with someone else. Lots of copies keeps stuff safe, after all; if you think you have friends whoâd like to hold on to a copy of whatever site youâve backed it up, pass it along and share the duty of preserving it! If any of this sounds interesting to you, Iâd encourage you to at least give it a try. Iâd love for the world to be filled with thousands upon thousands of little web archives, with people and community groups archiving and sharing the things that matter to them for themselves. If youâre finding any of this overwhelming, and youâre not sure where to get started, please reach out to me - Iâm very happy to give you a hand. The appeal to me is, I hope, obvious.Â ↩ Most of the tools Iâm mentioning also use the WACZ format, which packages up WARC files along with extra metadata.Â ↩ For those who want a little extra technical detail, though: one of the things that makes WARC special is that it records complete information about requests and responses, including all headers. This gives WARC a much more complete view of the whole process of visiting a website, and makes it possible to archive even complicated sites with client-side JavaScript that make a ton of requests.Â ↩ Posted by Misty De Meo Oct 29 th , 2026 4:21 pm archives « Performing digital surgery to fix MIDIs for my hardware (and then discovering the entire premise of my post was wrong) Recent Posts If you love a website, back it up Performing digital surgery to fix MIDIs for my hardware (and then discovering the entire premise of my post was wrong) What's up with that song from the duck game on Amiga CD32 anyway? title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
body_text: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights on this site; this gives it the look of the it is in the source --> , an SVG cannot use the page's web fonts and falls back to Helvetica, so each one is put into the page itself: its text is then set in Source Sans 3 and JetBrains Mono like the rest. If the file cannot be fetched (the page opened as a file), the stays. --> Rikiya Takehi News Publications Blog Experience CV 日本語 Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights Authors Rikiya Takehi * Jayden Teoh * Alex Zhang Omar Khattab Affiliations MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL Published November 2, 2026 TL;DR We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing. These results show sparks of Weight-Space Programming, which may extend beyond what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability. Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights . Read Which game was this neural network trained on? Astra reads the 17,253 weights, with no tools Breakout 99% confident Fix A trained policy never gets the car over the strip. Astra edits 3.5% of the weights, in one shot 100% success, up from 0% Improve Make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math. 7.9% base 7.9% Astra’s edit Astra edits the weights in a Python kernel, with no training 48.1% on MATH-500, up from 7.9% If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible. Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals. Weight-Space Programming For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models . We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms. In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks . In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all. In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models: LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic. LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too. LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go. Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers. In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights. Experiment 1 Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights? We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read. For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from. Setup Games: our own grid versions of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway, all on the same 10×10 grid with the same five actions Network: MLP 500 → 32 → 32 → 5, tanh (17,253 weights), the same for every game Input: the 10×10 grid in 5 channels: agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, previous frame Output: 5 action logits: no-op, up, down, left, right Training: PPO, 1 billion steps, the same settings for every game, the best of 3 seeds per game Astra gets: all the weights as text, and the grid and actions described without any game named It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart. Experiment 2 Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate? Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models. We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes. Setup Models: three diffusion models (DDPM) of 12×12 grayscale images, one each for filled circles, squares and triangles Network: MLP 160 → 64 → 64 → 144, ReLU (23,824 weights) Input: a noisy image (144 pixels) and the diffusion step (16 numbers) Output: the clean image (144 pixels) Training: Adam, 40,000 steps, batch 512 Astra gets: all the weights as text, with no shape named, and is told not to compute any forward pass Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights. Experiment 3 Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone? Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers. We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python code The Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub . , Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input. We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does . Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one. Trained on Astra’s answer (& confidence), two attempts Copying heads Astra names (layer.head) Copying heads, ground truth Python Python (0.56), Python (0.52) 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 Romaji romaji (0.55), romaji (0.62) 3.3 3.3 English English (0.58), English (0.48) 3.1 3.1 Where the copying heads are … tot al … tot al A copying head finds the same letters earlier in the text and copies what came after them. copying head other head Rows are layers 0 to 3, columns are heads 0 to 5 Astra: from the weights. Measured: by running the model Python Astra Measured Romaji Astra Measured English Astra Measured Figure 1: The copying heads Astra read from the weights match the measured ones in all three models. Setup Models: character-level transformers, 4 layers × 6 heads, width 384 (7.16 million weights), 28 characters: a–z, space and newline Training: 1 billion characters each, of Python code, Japanese literature in romaji (Aozora Bunko), or English Wikipedia Astra gets: the weights of the four transformer blocks only, with no input layer, no output layer and no labels on the 384 dimensions, and Python to analyze them, up to 100 runs Not allowed: running the network or any of its layers on any input, real, random or made up, and search. We checked every run Asked: which of the three texts the network was trained on, and what each head does Truth: each head measured by running the network on a random string repeated twice. Copying heads score 0.22 to 0.55, every other head at most 0.02. Astra never sees this The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to tot al when tot al came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along ( Figure 1 ). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python. Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x. Can an LLM write neural network weights? So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights. Experiment 4 Can Astra fix a failing network by editing its weights? We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck. We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights. Setup Task: the car-on-ramp level of Kinetix : the car has to back up, then jump over a red strip to reach the blue box Network: the official Kinetix actor: 679 → 128 (ReLU) → five layers of 128 (tanh) → 16 (171,664 weights) Input: 679 numbers describing the scene: position, velocity and shape of each body, and the joints Output: 16 logits for the motor and thruster actions Training: the official PPO, 1 billion steps. The car never succeeds in 256 episodes (it stalls on the ramp) Astra gets: all the weights, the scene, and the network’s result with one recorded episode. It is asked to explain the failure and fix only its cause, in one reply From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest. Experiment 5 Can the LLM write weights from scratch? Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot. We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network. Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest. Game PPO, 100M steps PPO, 500M steps Astra, one-shot Breakout 15.8 25.3 517.4 Seaquest 5.6 88.9 53.1 Asterix 25.8 55.2 53.2 Setup Games: Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix from MinAtar , on a 10×10 grid Network: 600 → 32 → 32 → 6 (tanh), the same shape as the PPO networks, every weight starting at 0 Input and output: the grid in 6 channels (player, danger, reward, projectile, trail, gauge), and 6 action logits Astra gets: the game’s rules and source code, the input and output layout, and how the network is scored Training: none: no data, no loss, no gradients, and no tools. Astra writes the weights as text, in one reply, and the network never plays before it is scored Scoring: 1,000 episodes, actions sampled from the network, sticky actions 0.1, at most 10,000 steps. PPO: the best of 3 to 10 seeds How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position. Real-World Relevant Scenarios (Scaling Up and Tool-use) So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space. From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space. Experiment 6 Writing a Go algorithm We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access. Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes. We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes. With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games. Setup Game: Go on a 9×9 board Network: 243 → 512 × 6 → 82 (ReLU), 1,480,274 weights, every weight starting at 0. Input: the stones of each side and whose turn it is. Output: one logit per point and one for passing. Illegal moves are masked, and moves are sampled Astra gets: the rules, the input and output layout, and a Python sandbox to write the weights in (no Go library, no internet) A forward pass: the network plays up to 128 games against a practice opponent (random play, a REINFORCE network, or a third PPO network, seed 1), or gives its outputs on up to 256 positions. 0 forward passes: one Python run, then the answer Not allowed: training or fitting the weights to data, search (no tree search, no rollouts), and running the network outside the forward passes Scoring: 2,000 games against each of two small PPO networks (seeds 0 and 2, 243 → 32 → 32 → 82, 20,000 iterations of 1,024 games), which Astra never plays, as Black in half, moves sampled How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more. Experiment 7 Which language model is sycophantic? Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly. We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA dataset The QA dataset: GitHub . . One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning. Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained. Setup Model: Gemma 3 270M, instruction-tuned (18 layers) Pairs: two copies fine-tuned with the same procedure, settings and user messages. One gives the correct answer, the other the user’s guess. The token embedding is frozen, so it is the same in both. Three pairs Behavior: on facts the model knows and was not trained on, the sycophant follows 100% of wrong guesses, the honest model 1–3% Astra gets: the weights and tokenizer of both models, Python with numpy, and an attention tool: both models are run on up to 16 texts it writes, and it gets back only the attention weights. It may not run the models itself. At most 20 runs Asked: which model is the sycophant, and which layers, heads and MLPs carry the difference It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion ( Figure 2 ). Where head 10.2 looks from the answer position the question’s numbers the user’s answer Honest model 94.3% 0.75% Sycophant 3.5% 85.7% Figure 2: In the sycophant, head 10.2 looks at the user’s answer instead of the question’s numbers. Experiment 8 Make a language model better at math Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights. We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed. Setup Model: Qwen3.5-0.8B, thinking on (24 layers, 0.8 billion weights) Task: make it better at math by editing its weights directly, with no gradient descent and no training Astra gets: a Python kernel over the weights (no GPU), practice problems (7,469 from GSM8K and 7,275 from MATH, not the test sets), and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes (a forward pass: the model answers up to 512 problems, or reads up to 1,024 texts) Evaluation: MATH-500, GSM8K and six other benchmarks, thinking on, up to 32,768 tokens. Astra never sees them Sampling: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, presence penalty 1.5. Qwen’s model card notes that this model is prone to thinking loops. Each score averages several samples per problem: 16 on AMC23, 4 on MATH-500, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench and GPQA Diamond, 2 on GSM8K and IFEval, and 1 on MMLU-Pro (a fixed 1,000 of its questions) As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights . With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%. Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 (%) GSM8K (%) IFEval (%) Hit token limit (%) Base 7.9 13.8 21.0 93.0 Edited, 10 forward passes 12.3 25.7 49.0 87.2 Edited, 25 forward passes 14.1 25.1 39.9 86.4 Edited, 50 forward passes 48.1 67.1 62.3 33.1 Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining. Additional experiment Raising math capability of a model that does not loop Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem. Gemma 3 270M MATH-500 (%) Base 6.8 Edited, 5 forward passes 7.0 Edited, 10 forward passes 7.6 Edited, 25 forward passes 7.7 Edited, 50 forward passes 7.0 Background and Related Works Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly. Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them . On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools. What Comes Next? In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization. This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples: Auditing without evaluation: This may allow us to uncover hidden problems or capabilities without ever running inference or benchmarks. Currently, capabilities and vulnerabilities can only be detected if we have test sets designed for them, or worse, after deployment in the real world. If LLMs can interpret weight space accurately, we could identify such issues directly from the weights (e.g., backdoors). Dramatically reducing optimization cost: Weight-space editing could save immense time and compute. For instance, one-shot model initialization would be far faster and more efficient than curating datasets and running full training loops. Zero-data capability steering and unlearning: Adding or unlearning a capability currently requires extensive data collection and fine-tuning. In the future, we may just prompt “Can you add Capability X to the model?” and the LLM can directly tweak some weights. Because such an edit touches only a few weights (0.016% in Experiment 8), it can leave the rest of the model intact and avoid the catastrophic forgetting that fine-tuning often causes. Recursive self-improvement: Today, recursive self-improvement is often operationalized as a model writing code that launches training jobs. An LLM that can inspect, debug, and improve its own weights, or those of a newer model, offers a richer, more native path to it. True architectural and model merging: Today, merging models relies on averaging weights, which only works for models with identical architectures. An LLM that understands the weight space could instead graft a circuit, such as a reasoning module, from one model into a completely different one, without retraining. We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline. Logs We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number. The edited Qwen3.5-0.8B from Experiment 8 is on Hugging Face . We thank Ahsen Khaliq at Hugging Face for rebuilding it from these logs, re-running its evaluation, and making a live demo . Acknowledgements Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty , Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab , Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations! Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project. body_text: Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432 · freenode free node IRC About ◐ Kernel Distros Desktop Internet Web Languages Infra Security Cryptocurrency AI Policy Self-Hosted Digests Self-Hosted By relay October 31, 2026 Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432 No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating. L Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update. Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables. Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. Solopreneur? NIST Has a Cybersecurity Guide Just for You November 2, 2026 Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email A new NIST guide can help solo business owners — also called “solopreneurs” — grasp the basics of cybersecurity and craft a strategy that can help reduce their cybersecurity risk. The guide is designed to help solopreneurs prioritize and implement a selection of actions from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework that would best help their businesses. The publication is written in lay language and assumes no prior cybersecurity knowledge. Credit: Asian Isolated/Shutterstock If you work for yourself, as millions of Americans do, protecting your business from cyberattack is one of many responsibilities that falls entirely on your shoulders. Don’t feel daunted: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has just released a guide with your needs — and busy life — in mind. Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 50) is a lay-language resource offering cybersecurity basics tailored expressly to the “solopreneur” — a term referring to anyone who is a business’s sole paid employee. More than 28 million small businesses in the U.S. fall into the solopreneur category, existing in every industry and forming a substantial part of the economy. The publication is written to introduce solopreneurs to the fundamentals of a small-business cybersecurity program and provide an actionable approach to implementing it. “Because solopreneurs may not have cybersecurity expertise, we wanted to create a resource designed for them,” said NIST’s Daniel Eliot, one of the publication’s authors. “They can implement many of these actions on their own with limited technical knowledge or with minimal financial investment.” The publication is an update to what was previously titled Small Business Information Security: The Fundamentals ( NISTIR 7621 ). While that publication was aimed at small businesses of varying sizes and covered the broader topic of information security, the revision is narrower in scope and concentrates on protecting digital systems from malicious attack. The updated publication draws its guidelines from the well-known NIST Cybersecurity Framework ( CSF 2.0 ), though the new publication is written with the novice in mind. “This publication assumes the reader has no familiarity with cybersecurity or the NIST CSF,” Eliot said. “We want to educate people about what cybersecurity is and how it fits in with a successful business plan. We know solopreneurs are often very busy people, so any time we introduce a topic or throw out jargony terms, we try to provide context and definitions for the lay reader.” The publication’s opening section, which includes the introduction and a chapter on the NIST CSF, is essentially a primer on cybersecurity and how it can support a solopreneur’s business. “In addition to the general context, we highlight a set of actionable best practices that significantly reduce cybersecurity risks. These include regular data backups and maintaining updated software,” Eliot said. “They are a good set of first steps a small business might take.” The central section offers specific actions from the CSF that can be implemented in a solo business. For each of these actions, the guide includes the rationale for performing it, how the business can get started, and options for what to do later as the business grows. Each action offers a brief citation that maps to the relevant section in the CSF and often references additional resources, so that interested readers can learn more. For example, one recommended action is to change the default passwords that a manufacturer assigns to a device, as is common with Wi-Fi routers and other networked items. The rationale is that criminals can easily find these default passwords and use them to access the device. The business can get started by reviewing the security settings on all devices and creating unique, strong passwords for them. As the business grows, it can establish procedures for device onboarding and management to ensure it manages passwords securely. Closing the document is a set of tools to help with implementing the central section’s actions, such as worksheets for inventorying at-risk assets or tracking all the actions the business has taken. Included here are three “use cases” — hypothetical solopreneurs including a lawyer, an artisan and a business consultant — that can help solopreneurs visualize and plan their own cybersecurity strategy. “Working through these guidelines can help a solopreneur develop a strong foundation in cybersecurity,” Eliot said. “The publication is not comprehensive and won’t address all the needs of every solopreneur, because every reader will have different levels of cybersecurity knowledge and sophistication. But it does provide a good starting point for solo business owners that need one.” Information technology , Cybersecurity and privacy , Identity and access management and Risk management Media Contact Chad Boutin [email protected] (301) 975-4261 NIST in your inbox Stay up to date with the latest news from NIST. title: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
body_text: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack | Sweden | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 3 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Wordiply Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail 1:15 'It's a form of terrorism': fridges across Europe hit by suspected cyber-attacks – video Sweden Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? Jon Henley Europe correspondent Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.39 EST First published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.12 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France. Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg , the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked. The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros. A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”. An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”. View image in fullscreen Workers at ICA’s Sjöbo shop empty fridges of spoiled produce. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/Reuters The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters. The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit. It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.” A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries. View image in fullscreen Empty fridges in a Delhaize supermarket near Brussels. Photograph: Maude Brulard/AFP/Getty Images Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets. “We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.” He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges? Read more “It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly. Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result. In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected. At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster. “This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected. Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale. View image in fullscreen A customer surveys an empty refrigerator at a SuperValu supermarket in Dublin. Photograph: Reuters Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said. “Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters. Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said. “Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.” In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates. The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate. The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility. title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
body_text: The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public | TechPolicy.Press Home Topics Newsletter Podcast Series Contributors About Donate Perspective The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public Matt Scherer / Nov 2, 2026 Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts . Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images) Republish Share Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies. That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut. The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is. Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer. Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due. The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models. Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so. Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts , Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments. Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic. Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins AI industry margins Demand pressure: Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI. Commoditization: Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices. Cost pressures: High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash. External constraints: Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation. AI industry margins Demand pressure: Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI. Commoditization: Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices. Cost pressures: High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash. External constraints: Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation. Source: Matthew U. Scherer and Maya Jenkins, “Brace for Impact: Protecting People and the Economy When the AI Bubble Bursts,” Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, October 2026 (Figure 13, p. 30). Interactive graphic: Tech Policy Press First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies , including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses . Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%). Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid . Our content delivered to your inbox. Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy Subscribe Loading... Thank you! You have successfully joined our subscriber list. Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential. In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required. That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion , and the prices for some components are soaring. That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments. And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task. Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher. Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost. If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash ; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice. It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “ on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect .” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches. The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy. HDMI-CEC switches aren't KVM switches that only do HDMI. An HDMI-CEC switcher box (or devices with that functionality built into them, like many soundbars) doesn't act as its own isolated sub-HDMI-CEC bus, where the switch presents to its downstreams as the root HDMI-CEC device, catching (without bubbling) <Active Source> messages from said downstreams, selecting one downstream to be active in an internal sense, and then presenting itself to its upstream connected TV or what-have-you as if it's one leaf-node source whose video+audio signals just-so-happen to be those of the currently-selected downstream. Rather, at an HDMI-CEC level, an HDMI switch is a lot more like a USB switch: it passes through all the CEC message broadcasts from all of its downstream source devices through to its upstream receiver device (and vice-versa), sometimes also interpreting them in turn for effect; and the root host device can actually see the whole tree topology, including any switches. (Fun fact: HDMI-CEC devices have four-step hierarchical addresses, that look like IP addresses, describing at each step the physical socket-number offset on the upstream device that connects said upstream to the given downstream. The TV is always 0.0.0.0. Whatever's plugged into the TV's first HDMI socket is 1.0.0.0. If that thing is an HDMI switcher box, then whatever's plugged into its first downstream HDMI socket is 1.1.0.0. And so on. All of these devices can see and talk to one another using these addresses, at all times. It's a network!) Importantly, this means that if a TV is plugged into an HDMI switcher box, which in turn has several source devices plugged into it, then the TV will still be aware of , and can still hear and speak to , all the inactive sources downstream of the switcher box, not just the active one. Which in turn means that if your TV is really stupid in the way it handles HDMI-CEC (e.g. trying to "argue" with sources about who's supposed to be active on wake, with the TV trying to force the last-active source and the source that woke the TV trying to force itself as the active source), then putting an HDMI-CEC switcher box in between will by no means improve things. They'll still be arguing, now "through" the switcher box; and the switcher box will itself be doing additional things in response to seeing these messages. Where previously you had O(N) HDMI-CEC problems, now you'll have O(N log N) HDMI-CEC problems. But hey, at least your leaf-node sources in this tree all show up in the TV's input switcher menu! That was definitely worth making all this mess, HDMI Forum! :P reply andrewla 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I've never really dug into it but this does explain a lot of the strange and flakey behavior that I've seen with switches purporting to offer HDMI-CEC support. You can't do it from a peer device; you can't do it from a "man in the middle" like a switch; and you can't even do it from the TV. Why? Because the HDMI-CEC bus protocol, as it stands today, has no separation of responsibilities/phases between "request" and "response" messages, or between "command" and "event" messages. Imagine how you or any other reasonable person would design HDMI-CEC. There'd be one "leader" device (probably the TV) whose opinion on the current active source / signal-path is canonical for the whole bus. Other devices would send command messages to this leader device to get it to change the active source. The leader could ACK or NACK these command messages. If the leader accepts the change, the leader would broadcast an event message declaring to the bus what the new canonical active source is. And if a device misses that message, it could also query the leader device to find out the active source. But that's not how any of this works. Instead, at any time, any device on the bus can just outright say "I'm the active source now." And every other device on the bus that receives this packet, must then update their own internal HDMI-CEC state-machines to consider that device to be active. If something (the TV, say) disagrees with this assertion, it can't just ignore the packet, because everything else on the bus won't have ignored it. And 1.0.0.0 might have gone to sleep in response to seeing the message that 3.1.0.0 is now active. Etc. The only legal thing a device that wants to "prevent another device from making itself the active source" can do , under HDMI-CEC, is to steal focus right back to itself (or, if it's a TV, assign focus right back to the source it remembers.) Which means everything on a bus sees the active source flapping back and forth. The different radios on a Smart TV viz. OTA, WiFi, Bluetooth, Satellite, Zigbee etc. all operate at different frequency ranges and hence need their own antennas. To replace the default launcher on a TCL TV using ADB, you must first install a third-party launcher (such as Projectivy Launcher or FLauncher) and then disable the stock Google TV launcher packages via command line. 1. Enable Developer Options and ADB Navigate to Settings > System > About and click Android TV OS Build or Build Number seven times to unlock Developer Options. Then, go to Settings > System > Developer Options and enable USB Debugging (and Network Debugging if using wireless ADB). 2. Connect via ADB Connect your computer to the TV's IP address using the terminal: # adb connect <TV_IP_ADDRESS> 3. Disable Stock Launcher and Setup Wizard Run the following commands to disable the default Google TV launcher and the setup wizard (which often reverts changes on reboot): # adb shell pm disable-user --user 0 com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx # adb shell pm disable-user --user 0 com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith Note: On some newer TCL models running Android 14, you may need to temporarily disable the package installer (com.android.packageinstaller) to sideload APKs, or manually select the new launcher via the Home button prompt after disabling the stock launcher. 4.
